title: Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search
description: This module introduces students to fundamental graph traversal algorithms that form the backbone of many computational solutions in computer science. Graph algorithms are essential for solving problems in network analysis, pathfinding, social media platforms, web crawling, and artificial intelligence. Students will explore Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithms, understanding their implementation, time and space complexity, and practical applications. The module emphasizes hands-on coding experience with real-world scenarios such as finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs, detecting cycles, and exploring connected components. Through interactive coding exercises and visual demonstrations, students will develop intuition for when to apply each algorithm and how graph representation affects performance. This foundation prepares students for advanced topics in algorithms, network theory, and machine learning, while building critical problem-solving skills that directly transfer to technical interviews and software development roles.
learning_objectives: Students will implement both BFS and DFS algorithms in Python by writing complete, working code that traverses adjacency lists and adjacency matrices
Students will analyze algorithm efficiency through calculating and comparing time and space complexity of BFS versus DFS for different graph structures
Students will solve real-world problems using appropriate graph traversal algorithms, including shortest path finding, cycle detection, and connected component identification
key_concepts: Breadth-First Search (BFS) - systematic level-by-level graph exploration using queues, guaranteeing shortest path in unweighted graphs
Depth-First Search (DFS) - recursive graph exploration that goes as deep as possible before backtracking, useful for topological sorting and cycle detection
Graph representations - adjacency lists and adjacency matrices with their respective memory usage and access time trade-offs
Queue and Stack data structures - FIFO and LIFO mechanisms that enable BFS and DFS implementations respectively
Time complexity analysis - O(V + E) performance characteristics where V represents vertices and E represents edges
prerequisite_concepts: Basic data structures: arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues with implementation knowledge
Graph theory fundamentals: vertices, edges, directed vs undirected graphs, and basic graph terminology
Recursion concepts and recursive function implementation
Big O notation and algorithm complexity analysis
Python programming proficiency including list manipulation and object-oriented concepts
readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 22 'Elementary Graph Algorithms' (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 594-630
Journal article: 'Graph Traversal Algorithms and Their Applications' (Zhang & Kumar, 2023) - focus on sections 2.1-2.3 covering BFS/DFS optimizations
Online resource: VisuAlgo Graph Traversal - interactive BFS/DFS visualizations and step-through examples
LeetCode Problems: #200 Number of Islands, #133 Clone Graph - practical algorithm application exercises
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours coding activities, 3 hours programming assignments)
summary: This module provides students with essential graph traversal skills that are fundamental to computer science problem-solving. By mastering BFS and DFS, students gain powerful tools for navigating and analyzing connected data structures that appear throughout software development, from social networks to game AI. The hands-on implementation experience builds coding confidence while the complexity analysis develops critical thinking about algorithm efficiency. These skills directly support advanced coursework in algorithms, artificial intelligence, and systems design, while also preparing students for technical interviews where graph problems are commonly featured. The module's emphasis on practical applications ensures students understand not just how these algorithms work, but when and why to use them in real-world scenarios.

title: Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables offer average-case O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for efficient algorithm design and system implementation. Students will examine the mathematical foundations of hash functions, analyze different collision resolution techniques, and implement working hash table solutions. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical application, covering real-world scenarios where hash tables are critical, such as database indexing, caching systems, compiler symbol tables, and password storage. Students will gain hands-on experience with various hashing algorithms, load factor management, and performance optimization techniques. By the end of this module, learners will understand when and how to effectively utilize hash tables in software development, recognize trade-offs between different implementation strategies, and be able to design custom hash functions for specific use cases. This knowledge is crucial for technical interviews, system design, and building scalable software applications.

Students will design custom hash functions using modular arithmetic and bitwise operations for string and numeric data types
key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps input data to fixed-size integer values, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods
Load Factor - The ratio of occupied slots to total slots in a hash table, critical for maintaining performance and determining when to resize
Universal Hashing - A randomized approach to hash function selection that provides theoretical guarantees about expected collision behavior
Open Addressing - Collision resolution method where colliding elements are stored in alternative locations within the same array using probing sequences

title: Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of shortest path algorithms, fundamental components in computer science that solve optimization problems across diverse applications from GPS navigation to network routing protocols. Students will master three essential algorithms: Dijkstra's algorithm for weighted graphs with non-negative edges, the Bellman-Ford algorithm for handling negative weights, and the Floyd-Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, connecting mathematical concepts to real-world problem-solving. Through hands-on coding exercises, students will implement these algorithms from scratch and analyze their time and space complexities. The content bridges abstract algorithmic thinking with concrete applications in transportation networks, social media platforms, and distributed systems. By examining trade-offs between different approaches, students develop critical thinking skills essential for algorithm selection in professional software development. This module serves as a cornerstone for advanced topics in artificial intelligence, network analysis, and optimization theory.

key_concepts: Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths from single source in non-negative weighted graphs with O(V²) or O(E log V) complexity
Bellman-Ford Algorithm - Dynamic programming solution detecting negative cycles while computing shortest paths in O(VE) time complexity
Floyd-Warshall Algorithm - All-pairs shortest path solution using dynamic programming matrix with O(V³) complexity for dense graphs
Graph Representation - Adjacency matrix vs adjacency list trade-offs for memory usage and algorithm efficiency
Relaxation Process - Edge weight update mechanism central to shortest path computation and convergence proof

Students will master three essential algorithms: Dijkstra's algorithm for single-source shortest paths in weighted graphs, the Bellman-Ford algorithm for handling negative edge weights, and the Floyd-Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, covering time complexity analysis, algorithm correctness proofs, and real-world applications. Through hands-on coding exercises and problem-solving scenarios, students will develop proficiency in selecting appropriate algorithms based on graph characteristics and performance requirements. This knowledge forms a critical foundation for advanced topics in network optimization, distributed systems, and artificial intelligence, making it essential for computer science students pursuing careers in software engineering, data science, or systems architecture.
learning_objectives: Students will implement Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, and Floyd-Warshall algorithms by writing complete, tested code solutions in Python
Students will analyze algorithm complexity and correctness through mathematical proofs and empirical testing with various graph structures
Students will solve real-world shortest path problems using appropriate algorithm selection based on graph properties and constraints
key_concepts: Dijkstra's Algorithm: Greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths from a single source in non-negative weighted graphs
Bellman-Ford Algorithm: Dynamic programming technique that detects negative cycles while computing shortest paths from a single source
Floyd-Warshall Algorithm: All-pairs shortest path algorithm using dynamic programming with O(V³) time complexity
Relaxation: Process of updating distance estimates by comparing current path costs with newly discovered shorter alternatives
Priority Queue/Heap: Data structure essential for efficiently selecting minimum-distance vertices in Dijkstra's algorithm
prerequisite_concepts: Graph theory fundamentals: vertices, edges, weighted graphs, adjacency lists and matrices
Data structures: arrays, linked lists, heaps, and priority queues
Algorithm analysis: Big O notation, time and space complexity
Dynamic programming principles and recurrence relations
Basic proof techniques: induction and contradiction

summary: This module equips students with essential algorithmic problem-solving skills by mastering shortest path algorithms that appear frequently in technical interviews and real-world applications. Students gain hands-on experience implementing complex algorithms, analyzing their performance characteristics, and making informed decisions about algorithm selection based on problem constraints. The combination of theoretical rigor and practical coding experience prepares students for advanced coursework in algorithms, artificial intelligence, and systems design. key_concepts: Augmented Matrix - A rectangular array combining coefficient matrix and constants vector to represent a linear system in compact form

Coefficient Matrix - The square or rectangular matrix containing only the variable coefficients from a linear system
Back Substitution - The process of solving for variables starting from the bottom row of an upper triangular system

Students will transition from basic algebraic substitution methods to more sophisticated matrix-based approaches that are essential for advanced mathematics, engineering, and data science. The module emphasizes both computational skills and conceptual understanding, showing how linear systems appear in optimization problems, network analysis, and economic modeling. Through hands-on practice with augmented matrices, row operations, and solution interpretation, students will develop proficiency in identifying unique solutions, infinite solutions, and inconsistent systems. This foundation is crucial for linear algebra, differential equations, and numerical methods courses. The module balances theoretical understanding with practical problem-solving skills, preparing students to tackle complex multi-variable problems in their academic and professional careers.
learning_objectives: Students will solve systems of 2x2 and 3x3 linear equations by applying Gaussian elimination and back-substitution methods
Students will classify solution types (unique, infinite, no solution) through analyzing augmented matrices in row echelon form
Students will model real-world scenarios using systems of linear equations and interpret solutions within practical contexts
key_concepts: Gaussian Elimination: Systematic method using elementary row operations to transform augmented matrices into row echelon form
Augmented Matrix: Rectangular array combining coefficient matrix and constant vector to represent a linear system
Row Echelon Form: Matrix configuration with leading 1's and zeros below, enabling straightforward back-substitution
Solution Classification: Distinguishing between consistent systems (unique or infinite solutions) and inconsistent systems (no solution)
Elementary Row Operations: Three reversible matrix transformations (row swapping, scalar multiplication, row addition) that preserve solution sets
prerequisite_concepts: Solving linear equations in one and two variables using algebraic methods
Basic understanding of coordinate systems and graphing linear equations
Fundamental arithmetic operations with fractions and decimals
Substitution and elimination methods for simple 2x2 systems

title: Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Analysis
description: This module introduces students to fundamental graph algorithms, focusing on traversal methods and shortest path algorithms. Graph algorithms form the backbone of many computer science applications, from social network analysis to GPS navigation systems, web crawling, and network routing protocols. Students will explore both depth-first search (DFS) and breadth-first search (BFS) as foundational traversal techniques, then advance to studying Dijkstra's algorithm and the Bellman-Ford algorithm for finding shortest paths. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, requiring students to code these algorithms from scratch and analyze their time and space complexities. Through hands-on programming exercises and real-world case studies, students will understand when to apply each algorithm and recognize their computational trade-offs. This knowledge is essential for technical interviews, advanced algorithms courses, and software engineering roles involving network analysis, route optimization, or any system requiring efficient graph processing.

Students will analyze shortest path problems through coding and testing both Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford algorithms on weighted graphs with varying edge configurations

Students will solve real-world problems through applying appropriate graph algorithms to scenarios like social network friend recommendations and GPS route planning
key_concepts: Graph representation using adjacency lists and adjacency matrices for efficient storage and traversal operations
Depth-First Search (DFS): recursive and iterative implementations for exploring graph nodes by going as deep as possible before backtracking
Breadth-First Search (BFS): level-by-level exploration using queues to find shortest paths in unweighted graphs
Dijkstra's Algorithm: greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edges
Bellman-Ford Algorithm: dynamic programming method to detect negative cycles and find shortest paths in graphs with negative edge weights
Time complexity analysis: understanding O(V + E) for BFS/DFS and O((V + E) log V) for Dijkstra's algorithm where V is vertices and E is edges
prerequisite_concepts: Data structures including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, and priority queues with implementation knowledge
Basic graph theory terminology: vertices, edges, directed/undirected graphs, weighted graphs, and connectivity concepts
Big O notation and complexity analysis for evaluating algorithm performance
Recursion principles and implementation techniques
Python programming proficiency including object-oriented programming and debugging skills

description: This module introduces students to systems of linear equations, a fundamental algebraic concept that bridges basic equation solving with advanced mathematical applications. Students will learn to identify, set up, and solve systems using multiple methods including graphing, substitution, and elimination. The module emphasizes real-world applications such as business optimization, resource allocation, and geometric problems. By working with two and three-variable systems, students develop critical thinking skills and learn to choose appropriate solution methods based on problem context. This topic serves as a gateway to linear algebra and prepares students for advanced mathematics courses. Through hands-on problem-solving activities, students will discover how mathematical systems model complex relationships in economics, engineering, and science. The module combines theoretical understanding with practical application, ensuring students can both perform calculations accurately and interpret solutions meaningfully in context.
learning_objectives: Students will solve systems of two and three linear equations by applying graphing, substitution, and elimination methods
Students will translate real-world scenarios into mathematical systems through guided practice with word problems
Students will determine the most efficient solution method using analysis of system characteristics and problem constraints
Students will interpret solutions in context by evaluating feasibility and meaning of results for practical applications
key_concepts: System of equations - A set of two or more equations with the same variables that must be solved simultaneously
Consistent system - A system that has at least one solution, which can be independent (unique solution) or dependent (infinite solutions)
Inconsistent system - A system with no solution, represented graphically by parallel lines
Substitution method - Solving one equation for a variable and substituting into other equations
Elimination method - Adding or subtracting equations to eliminate variables systematically
Break-even analysis - Business application finding where costs equal revenue using system solving
prerequisite_concepts: Solving single-variable linear equations and inequalities
Graphing linear equations using slope-intercept and standard forms
Understanding coordinate plane and interpreting intersection points
Basic algebraic manipulation including distributing and combining like terms
readings: Textbook chapter: College Algebra Systems and Matrices (Sullivan, 2019) pp. 156-198
Online resource: Khan Academy - Systems of Linear Equations module with interactive exercises
Application article: Linear Programming in Business Decision Making (Mathematics Teacher, 2020) - focus on real-world modeling
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (3 hours reading, 5 hours guided practice activities, 4 hours problem sets and application projects)
summary: This module establishes students' ability to work with multiple equations simultaneously, a skill essential for advanced mathematics and practical problem-solving. By mastering various solution methods, students gain flexibility in approach and develop mathematical reasoning. The emphasis on real-world applications demonstrates mathematics' relevance beyond the classroom while building critical thinking skills. Students will complete this module with confidence in setting up and solving systems, interpreting results meaningfully, and selecting appropriate methods for different problem types. These skills directly support success in subsequent topics including matrices, linear programming, and calculus applications involving optimization.

title: Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
description: This module introduces students to the fundamental concepts of algorithm analysis, focusing on time and space complexity evaluation using Big O notation. Students will learn to systematically analyze algorithms to predict their performance characteristics and make informed decisions about algorithm selection for specific problems. The module covers asymptotic notation, worst-case, average-case, and best-case analysis, and practical techniques for measuring algorithm efficiency. Understanding algorithm complexity is crucial for writing scalable software and optimizing system performance. Students will work with concrete examples, analyzing sorting algorithms, search algorithms, and basic data structure operations. This foundation is essential for advanced topics in data structures, software engineering, and system design, where performance considerations directly impact user experience and system scalability.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate time and space complexity for given algorithms by applying Big O, Theta, and Omega notations to nested loops, recursive functions, and iterative processes
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through hands-on analysis of sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) using both theoretical calculation and empirical measurement
Students will implement complexity analysis tools using Python profiling libraries to measure actual runtime performance and validate theoretical predictions
key_concepts: Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size
Space Complexity - Amount of memory space required by an algorithm during execution relative to input size
Asymptotic Analysis - Method of describing limiting behavior of functions when argument approaches infinity
Worst-case Analysis - Evaluation of algorithm performance under most challenging input conditions
prerequisite_concepts: Basic programming proficiency in at least one language (loops, functions, recursion)
Fundamental mathematical concepts including logarithms, exponents, and summation notation
Understanding of basic data structures (arrays, linked lists)
Elementary discrete mathematics and proof techniques
readings: Textbook chapter: 'Algorithm Analysis' from Introduction to Algorithms (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 43-84
Research paper: 'A Guide to Algorithm Design Paradigms' (Johnson, 2021) - focusing on complexity analysis methodology
Online resource: Khan Academy Algorithm Course - Big O Notation interactive modules and visualization tools
Documentation: Python time and cProfile modules official documentation for practical performance measurement
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours hands-on coding exercises, 3 hours complexity analysis assignments)
summary: This module establishes critical analytical skills for evaluating algorithm performance through systematic complexity analysis. Students gain practical experience measuring and predicting algorithm behavior, enabling them to make data-driven decisions in software development. The combination of theoretical understanding and hands-on measurement prepares students for advanced computer science topics including data structures, database optimization, and system design. These skills are immediately applicable in technical interviews, software engineering roles, and research contexts where performance optimization is paramount.

description: This module introduces students to Binary Search Trees (BSTs), a fundamental hierarchical data structure that enables efficient searching, insertion, and deletion operations. Students will explore the theoretical foundations of BSTs, understand their structural properties, and implement core operations from scratch. The module emphasizes both practical programming skills and algorithmic analysis, connecting tree traversal methods to real-world applications like database indexing and file systems. Through hands-on coding exercises and complexity analysis, students will gain deep insights into when BSTs are optimal choices versus alternative data structures. The module also addresses BST limitations, including worst-case scenarios and introduces concepts of tree balancing. This knowledge is crucial for software engineering roles, technical interviews, and advanced computer science topics like database management systems and compiler design. By mastering BSTs, students develop critical thinking skills for choosing appropriate data structures and understanding trade-offs between time and space complexity in algorithm design.

Students will analyze time and space complexity of BST operations through mathematical proof techniques and empirical testing with various input distributions

Successor/Predecessor: Next larger/smaller element in BST used for deletion of nodes with two children

Big O notation and algorithmic complexity analysis

title: Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies
description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Students will master the principles of hash function design, understand the mathematical foundations of load factors and performance analysis, and implement multiple collision resolution techniques. Hash tables are critical for database indexing, compiler symbol tables, caching systems, and countless real-world applications where O(1) average-case lookup time is essential. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, covering open addressing methods (linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing) and separate chaining approaches. Students will analyze the trade-offs between different collision resolution strategies, understand when hash tables degrade to O(n) performance, and learn to choose appropriate hash functions for different data types. Through hands-on coding exercises and performance benchmarking, students will gain the expertise needed to implement efficient hash-based solutions in software engineering roles and technical interviews.

key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across hash table indices
Load Factor - The ratio of number of stored elements to hash table size, directly affecting collision probability and performance
Linear Probing - An open addressing collision resolution method that searches for the next available slot sequentially
Separate Chaining - A collision resolution technique using linked lists or arrays at each hash table index to store multiple elements
Double Hashing - A collision resolution method using a second hash function to determine probe step size, reducing clustering

Hash tables offer average-case O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for building efficient software systems. Students will learn the mathematical foundations of hash functions, explore various collision resolution techniques, and analyze performance trade-offs in real-world scenarios. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation skills, covering open addressing methods (linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing) and chaining approaches. Through hands-on coding exercises and performance analysis, students will gain experience implementing hash tables from scratch and optimizing them for different use cases. This knowledge is crucial for technical interviews, systems programming, database design, and understanding the internals of programming language features like dictionaries, maps, and sets. The module also addresses security considerations, including cryptographic hash functions and protection against hash collision attacks.
learning_objectives: Students will implement a complete hash table with chaining collision resolution by writing modular C++ or Python code with proper encapsulation
Students will analyze and compare collision resolution strategies through empirical testing with datasets of varying sizes and distribution patterns
Students will design appropriate hash functions using mathematical techniques including the division method, multiplication method, and universal hashing
Students will evaluate hash table performance using load factor analysis and Big-O complexity assessment for different collision scenarios
key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
Load Factor - The ratio of occupied slots to total slots in a hash table, critical for performance analysis and resizing decisions
Collision Resolution - Systematic approaches to handle situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
Universal Hashing - A randomized technique for selecting hash functions that provides theoretical guarantees about worst-case performance
Dynamic Resizing - The process of growing or shrinking hash table capacity while maintaining data integrity and optimal load factors

description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Students will examine the theoretical foundations of hash functions, analyze various collision resolution strategies, and implement hash table operations from scratch. The module emphasizes both the mathematical principles underlying effective hash function design and the practical considerations for real-world applications. Through hands-on coding exercises and performance analysis, students will understand why hash tables achieve O(1) average-case performance for search, insertion, and deletion operations, while also learning to handle worst-case scenarios. The content covers essential topics including the division method, multiplication method, universal hashing, separate chaining, open addressing with linear and quadratic probing, and double hashing. Students will also explore load factor management and dynamic resizing strategies. This knowledge is crucial for software engineering roles, technical interviews, and advanced computer science coursework involving databases, compilers, and distributed systems.

Load Factor - The ratio of occupied slots to total slots in a hash table, critical for maintaining optimal performance and determining when to resize
Universal Hashing - A randomized approach to hash function selection that provides theoretical guarantees about expected performance regardless of input distribution

description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Students will learn how hash tables achieve average O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations through effective hash function design and collision resolution strategies. The module covers the mathematical foundations of hash functions, practical implementation considerations, and real-world applications in databases, caches, and programming language interpreters. Students will implement multiple hash table variants from scratch, analyze their performance characteristics, and understand trade-offs between different collision resolution techniques. This knowledge is essential for software engineers, as hash tables form the backbone of many critical systems including database indexing, compiler symbol tables, and distributed caching systems. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical programming skills, preparing students to make informed decisions about when and how to use hash tables effectively in their own projects.
learning_objectives: Students will implement a complete hash table with chaining collision resolution by writing C++ or Java code that handles dynamic resizing and load factor management
Students will analyze hash function quality through empirical testing of distribution uniformity and collision rates using statistical analysis tools
Students will compare performance characteristics of different collision resolution strategies using big-O analysis and experimental benchmarking
Students will design custom hash functions for specific data types through mathematical analysis of key characteristics and bit manipulation techniques
key_concepts: Hash Function: A mathematical function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size hash codes, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
Collision Resolution: Strategies for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same table index, including chaining and open addressing methods
Load Factor: The ratio of stored elements to table size that determines when to resize the hash table to maintain optimal performance
Universal Hashing: A family of hash functions with mathematical guarantees about collision probability, providing worst-case performance bounds
prerequisite_concepts: Arrays and dynamic memory allocation
Linked lists and pointer manipulation
Big-O notation and time complexity analysis
Basic probability and modular arithmetic
Object-oriented programming concepts (classes, inheritance)
readings: Textbook chapter: Introduction to Algorithms Chapter 11 - Hash Tables (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 253-285
Research paper: Universal Classes of Hash Functions (Carter & Wegman, 1979) - focus on theoretical foundations and mathematical proofs
Online resource: GeeksforGeeks Hash Table Implementation Guide - practical coding examples and optimization techniques
Technical article: Google's Swiss Table Design (Abseil Documentation, 2023) - modern high-performance hash table architecture

summary: Upon completing this module, students will possess both theoretical knowledge and practical skills in hash table implementation and optimization. They will understand how to select appropriate hash functions for different data types, implement efficient collision resolution strategies, and analyze the performance trade-offs between different approaches. This foundation prepares students for advanced topics in database systems, compiler design, and distributed computing where hash tables play crucial roles. The hands-on programming experience ensures students can confidently implement and debug hash table-based solutions in real software projects, while the analytical components develop critical thinking skills for evaluating and optimizing data structure performance in production systems.

title: Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design, Implementation, and Collision Resolution
description: This module explores hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables provide average-case O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for building efficient software systems. Students will examine the mathematical foundations of hash functions, understand different collision resolution strategies, and analyze performance characteristics under various conditions. The module covers practical implementation details including dynamic resizing, load factor management, and real-world applications in databases, caching systems, and programming language implementations. Through hands-on coding exercises, students will implement multiple hash table variants and compare their performance. Understanding hash tables is crucial for technical interviews, system design, and building scalable applications. This module bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical software engineering skills.

key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, ideally distributing inputs uniformly across the hash table
Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling cases when different keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods
Load Factor - The ratio of stored elements to total table capacity, critical for maintaining optimal performance and determining when to resize
Universal Hashing - A randomized approach to hash function selection that provides theoretical guarantees on expected performance
Dynamic Resizing - The process of expanding or shrinking hash table capacity while rehashing existing elements to maintain efficiency

Students will implement hash tables from scratch, analyze their performance characteristics, and explore real-world applications in database indexing, caching systems, and compiler symbol tables. title: Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
description: Dynamic programming is a fundamental algorithmic paradigm that solves complex problems by breaking them down into simpler subproblems and storing solutions to avoid redundant computations. This module explores the theoretical foundations and practical applications of dynamic programming, emphasizing the transition from recursive solutions to optimized memoized implementations. Students will master the identification of overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure properties, two key characteristics that make problems suitable for dynamic programming approaches. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithmic analysis, learners will implement classic dynamic programming solutions including the Fibonacci sequence, longest common subsequence, knapsack problems, and matrix chain multiplication. The module bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical software development skills, demonstrating how dynamic programming reduces exponential time complexity to polynomial time in many real-world scenarios. Understanding dynamic programming is crucial for technical interviews, competitive programming, and developing efficient algorithms in areas such as bioinformatics, operations research, and artificial intelligence. By the end of this module, students will confidently recognize dynamic programming opportunities and implement both top-down (memoization) and bottom-up (tabulation) solutions.

Students will analyze time and space complexity improvements using Big O notation to compare naive recursive solutions with dynamic programming optimizations
Students will solve classic dynamic programming problems including 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, and edit distance through structured coding assignments
key_concepts: Overlapping Subproblems: The property where a recursive algorithm solves the same subproblems multiple times, making it suitable for optimization through storage of intermediate results
Optimal Substructure: The characteristic where an optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems, enabling the build-up of solutions from smaller components

Memoization (Top-Down): A technique that stores the results of expensive function calls and returns cached results when the same inputs occur again, typically implemented using recursion with a lookup table
Tabulation (Bottom-Up): A method that builds solutions iteratively from the smallest subproblems up to the target problem, typically using arrays or matrices to store intermediate results
State Space: The set of all possible configurations or parameters that define unique subproblems in a dynamic programming solution

Big O notation and time/space complexity analysis

description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of fundamental graph algorithms that form the backbone of many computer science applications. title: Limits and Continuity: Building the Foundation of Calculus
description: This module introduces the fundamental concept of limits, which forms the cornerstone of differential and integral calculus. Students will explore the intuitive notion of approaching a value without necessarily reaching it, then formalize this understanding through epsilon-delta definitions and limit laws. The concept of continuity emerges naturally from limits, providing the mathematical framework for understanding smooth functions and their behaviors. Through graphical analysis, algebraic manipulation, and real-world applications, students will master techniques for evaluating limits of various function types, including rational functions, trigonometric functions, and piecewise functions. Special attention is given to indeterminate forms and L'Hôpital's rule as powerful problem-solving tools. Understanding limits is crucial for success in calculus, as derivatives and integrals are defined as specific types of limits. This module bridges the gap between precalculus algebra and advanced calculus concepts, establishing the rigorous mathematical thinking required for higher-level mathematics courses.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate limits of functions using algebraic techniques, graphical analysis, and limit laws by solving progressively complex limit problems involving rational, trigonometric, and exponential functions
Students will determine continuity of functions at specific points and over intervals through systematic application of the three-part continuity definition and identification of discontinuity types
Students will apply L'Hôpital's rule to resolve indeterminate forms using appropriate differentiation techniques and recognize when the rule applies versus alternative methods
key_concepts: One-sided limits: The behavior of a function as the input approaches a specific value from either the left or right side exclusively
Epsilon-delta definition: The formal mathematical definition of a limit using arbitrary small positive numbers to establish precise bounds
Continuity types: Classification of function behavior including removable discontinuities, jump discontinuities, and infinite discontinuities
Indeterminate forms: Expressions like 0/0 or ∞/∞ that require special techniques such as L'Hôpital's rule or algebraic manipulation to evaluate
Squeeze theorem: A method for finding limits by trapping a function between two other functions with known limits
prerequisite_concepts: Function composition and transformation including domain, range, and basic function families (polynomial, rational, trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic)
Algebraic manipulation skills including factoring, rationalizing expressions, and simplifying complex fractions
Coordinate geometry and graph interpretation including asymptote identification and function behavior analysis
readings: Textbook chapter: Limits and Continuity (Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th Ed.) pp. 87-156
Supplementary article: The Historical Development of the Limit Concept (Mathematical Association of America, 2019) - focus on intuitive versus formal approaches
Online resource: Khan Academy Limits and Continuity unit - interactive exercises and step-by-step video explanations for visual learners
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours practice problems and activities, 3 hours assignments and assessments)
summary: This module establishes the critical foundation for all of calculus by developing both intuitive understanding and formal mathematical rigor around limits and continuity. Students gain essential problem-solving skills through multiple approaches: graphical visualization, algebraic manipulation, and formal definitions. The mastery of limit evaluation techniques, including recognition of indeterminate forms and application of L'Hôpital's rule, prepares students for derivatives and integrals in subsequent modules. Understanding continuity provides the framework for analyzing function behavior and identifying where calculus techniques can be applied. These concepts connect directly to real-world applications in physics, engineering, and economics where rates of change and accumulation are fundamental. The mathematical reasoning developed here—moving from intuitive understanding to rigorous proof—models the thinking process essential for advanced mathematics courses and establishes the analytical mindset required for success in STEM fields.

title: Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Problems
description: This module explores fundamental graph algorithms essential for solving complex computational problems in computer science. Students will master breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS) traversal techniques, then advance to shortest path algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm and the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Graph algorithms form the backbone of numerous real-world applications including social network analysis, GPS navigation systems, network routing protocols, and web crawling. Understanding these algorithms is crucial for technical interviews at major technology companies and provides the foundation for more advanced topics in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and distributed systems. Through hands-on implementation and practical problem-solving, students will develop both theoretical understanding and practical coding skills. The module emphasizes algorithm complexity analysis, helping students make informed decisions about algorithm selection based on specific problem constraints. By the end of this module, students will confidently approach graph-based problems with a toolkit of proven algorithms and the analytical skills to evaluate their efficiency and appropriateness for different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will implement BFS and DFS algorithms by writing complete Python functions that traverse graphs represented as adjacency lists

Students will analyze algorithm complexity using Big O notation to compare time and space efficiency of different graph traversal approaches
Students will apply graph algorithms to practical problems through a capstone project involving route optimization or social network analysis
key_concepts: Breadth-First Search (BFS): Level-by-level graph traversal using queue data structure, optimal for finding shortest unweighted paths
Depth-First Search (DFS): Deep exploration of graph branches using stack or recursion, essential for topological sorting and cycle detection

title: Limits and Continuity of Functions
description: This module introduces students to the fundamental concepts of limits and continuity, which form the foundation of differential calculus. Students will explore how functions behave as they approach specific values, learning to evaluate limits algebraically and graphically. The concept of continuity builds naturally from limits, helping students understand when functions have breaks, jumps, or holes. These concepts are essential for understanding derivatives, integrals, and real-world applications such as instantaneous velocity, population growth models, and optimization problems. Through interactive graphing, algebraic manipulation, and practical problem-solving, students will develop both computational skills and conceptual understanding. This module bridges the gap between algebra and calculus, providing the theoretical framework necessary for advanced mathematical analysis. Students will work with polynomial, rational, trigonometric, and piecewise functions to build a comprehensive understanding of limiting behavior and function continuity.

Students will analyze continuity of functions through graphical interpretation and formal epsilon-delta definitions
Students will identify and classify discontinuities using limit notation and graphing technology
Students will solve real-world application problems involving limits using mathematical modeling and interpretation
key_concepts: One-sided limits: The behavior of a function as x approaches a value from the left or right side only
Continuity at a point: A function is continuous at x=a if the limit exists, the function value exists, and they are equal
Squeeze theorem: Method for evaluating limits by bounding a function between two simpler functions
Removable vs non-removable discontinuities: Classification of breaks in functions that can or cannot be 'fixed' by redefining the function
Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuous functions take on all values between any two function values
prerequisite_concepts: Function notation and evaluation, including composite and piecewise functions
Algebraic manipulation: factoring, rationalizing denominators, and simplifying complex fractions
Basic trigonometric functions and their properties
Graphing functions and interpreting graphical behavior

title: Limits and Continuity of Functions: Advanced Topics 1
description: This module introduces the fundamental concept of limits, which forms the cornerstone of calculus and advanced mathematical analysis. Students will explore how functions behave as their input values approach specific points, including cases where the function may not be defined at that point. The module covers epsilon-delta definitions, limit laws, and the critical connection between limits and continuity. Understanding limits is essential for grasping derivatives and integrals in subsequent calculus courses. Through graphical, numerical, and analytical approaches, students will develop intuition about limiting behavior while building rigorous mathematical reasoning skills. The module emphasizes real-world applications including instantaneous velocity, population growth models, and optimization problems. Students will work with rational functions, trigonometric functions, and piecewise functions to master limit evaluation techniques. Special attention is given to indeterminate forms and methods for resolving them, preparing students for L'Hôpital's rule in advanced courses.

key_concepts: One-sided limits: The behavior of a function as x approaches a value from the left (x → a⁻) or right (x → a⁺) side exclusively
Epsilon-delta definition: The formal mathematical definition stating that lim(x→a) f(x) = L if for every ε > 0, there exists δ > 0 such that |f(x) - L| < ε whenever 0 < |x - a| < δ
Continuity at a point: A function is continuous at x = a if three conditions are met: f(a) exists, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a)
Indeterminate forms: Expressions like 0/0, ∞/∞, or ∞ - ∞ that require special techniques such as factoring, rationalization, or algebraic manipulation to evaluate
prerequisite_concepts: Function notation, domain and range, and composition of functions
Algebraic manipulation including factoring polynomials, rationalizing expressions, and solving equations

The rigorous epsilon-delta approach builds mathematical maturity while practical applications demonstrate relevance to engineering, physics, and economics. Mastery of this module enables students to understand instantaneous rates of change, laying groundwork for derivatives, and provides the mathematical framework for understanding accumulation processes that lead to integration. The combination of graphical intuition, numerical investigation, and algebraic techniques creates a comprehensive understanding that supports success in advanced mathematics courses and quantitative disciplines.

title: Hash Tables: Design, Implementation, and Performance Analysis
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables offer average-case O(1) time complexity for insertions, deletions, and lookups, making them essential for efficient algorithm design. Students will dive deep into the mathematical foundations of hash functions, explore various collision resolution strategies, and analyze the trade-offs between space and time complexity. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation skills, covering real-world applications from database indexing to compiler symbol tables. Students will implement multiple hash table variants from scratch, gaining hands-on experience with memory management, performance optimization, and empirical analysis. Special attention is given to modern considerations such as cryptographic hash functions, distributed hash tables, and cache-friendly designs. By connecting hash table principles to contemporary challenges in big data processing, web caching, and distributed systems, this module demonstrates the enduring relevance of this classic data structure in modern computing environments.
learning_objectives: Students will design and implement at least three different hash functions by analyzing their mathematical properties and collision patterns using empirical testing
Students will evaluate collision resolution strategies through hands-on coding of separate chaining, linear probing, and quadratic probing implementations
Students will analyze hash table performance using big-O notation, load factor calculations, and benchmarking tools to compare theoretical and practical efficiency
key_concepts: Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps arbitrary-sized data to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across the hash table
Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods
Load Factor - Ratio of occupied slots to total slots in a hash table, critical for performance analysis and determining when to resize
Universal Hashing - Family of hash functions where any two distinct keys have low probability of collision, providing theoretical guarantees
Dynamic Resizing - Process of expanding or contracting hash table size based on load factor to maintain optimal performance
prerequisite_concepts: Arrays and dynamic array operations (insertion, deletion, resizing)
Linked lists and pointer manipulation for chaining implementations
Basic probability theory and modular arithmetic for hash function analysis
Big-O notation and asymptotic analysis for performance evaluation
Memory allocation and deallocation in chosen programming language

title: Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path and Minimum Spanning Trees
description: This module explores fundamental graph algorithms that solve critical real-world problems in computer science and engineering. Students will master the theory and implementation of shortest path algorithms (Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford) and minimum spanning tree algorithms (Kruskal's and Prim's). These algorithms form the backbone of network routing protocols, GPS navigation systems, social network analysis, and network infrastructure design. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding of algorithm correctness and efficiency, as well as practical implementation skills using appropriate data structures. Students will analyze time and space complexity, understand when to apply each algorithm based on graph properties, and implement solutions that handle edge cases such as negative weights and disconnected graphs. Through hands-on coding exercises and real-world case studies, students will develop the ability to recognize graph-based problems in various domains and select the most appropriate algorithmic approach. This module bridges theoretical computer science with practical software engineering, preparing students for technical interviews and advanced coursework in algorithms, networking, and distributed systems.

key_concepts: Shortest Path Problem: Finding the minimum-weight path between vertices in a weighted graph, fundamental to routing and navigation
Dijkstra's Algorithm: Greedy algorithm for finding shortest paths from a source vertex in graphs with non-negative edge weights
Bellman-Ford Algorithm: Dynamic programming approach that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles
Minimum Spanning Tree (MST): A tree that connects all vertices in a weighted graph with minimum total edge weight
Kruskal's Algorithm: MST algorithm that sorts edges and uses union-find to avoid cycles
Prim's Algorithm: MST algorithm that grows the tree from a starting vertex using a priority queue
Union-Find Data Structure: Efficient data structure for tracking connected components with path compression and union by rank

title: Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval
description: This module explores hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables provide average-case O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for applications requiring fast data access. Students will learn how hash functions transform keys into array indices, understand different collision resolution strategies, and analyze the trade-offs between time and space complexity. The module covers practical implementations in various programming languages and examines real-world applications including database indexing, caching systems, and compiler symbol tables. Students will gain hands-on experience implementing hash tables from scratch, comparing different hash functions, and optimizing performance through load factor management. This knowledge is crucial for software engineering interviews, system design, and building efficient algorithms. The module also addresses security considerations in hash function design and introduces cryptographic hash functions used in blockchain and data integrity verification.

key_concepts: Hash Function: A function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size values (hash codes) used as array indices
Collision Resolution: Techniques to handle when multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
Load Factor: The ratio of filled slots to total slots in a hash table, affecting performance and memory usage
Universal Hashing: A randomized approach to hash function selection that provides theoretical guarantees on average-case performance
Perfect Hashing: Hash functions that produce no collisions for a specific set of keys, used in static datasets

title: Linear Transformations and Matrix Representations
description: This module explores the fundamental concept of linear transformations and their matrix representations, bridging abstract linear algebra with practical computational applications. Students will discover how linear transformations preserve vector operations while enabling geometric transformations like rotations, reflections, and scaling. The module emphasizes the powerful connection between abstract mathematical functions and concrete matrix calculations, showing how any linear transformation can be completely characterized by its matrix representation. Through visual demonstrations and computational exercises, students will understand how linear transformations form the backbone of computer graphics, data analysis, and engineering applications. The module builds intuition through geometric interpretations while developing technical skills in matrix operations, eigenvalue analysis, and transformation composition. By connecting theoretical concepts to real-world applications like image processing and 3D graphics, students will appreciate how linear transformations serve as essential tools across STEM fields. This foundation prepares students for advanced topics in differential equations, optimization, and machine learning where linear transformations are fundamental.

key_concepts: Linear Transformation: A function T: V → W between vector spaces that preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication (T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u))
Matrix Representation: The unique matrix [T] that encodes a linear transformation T, where each column contains the image of a basis vector under T
Kernel and Image: The kernel (null space) contains vectors mapped to zero; the image (range) contains all possible output vectors of the transformation
Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: Special scalars λ and vectors v where T(v) = λv, revealing the transformation's fundamental directional behaviors
prerequisite_concepts: Matrix operations including multiplication, inverse, and determinant calculation

Coordinate systems and vector representations in R^n

key_concepts: Depth-First Search (DFS) - A graph traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack data structure (explicit or recursive call stack)

Traversal tree - The tree structure formed by the edges used during graph traversal, which differs from the original graph and depends on the starting vertex and algorithm choice
Connected components - Maximal sets of vertices in an undirected graph where each vertex is reachable from every other vertex in the same component

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) with JavaScript
description: Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing functionality. This module introduces students to the TDD cycle of Red-Green-Refactor, where developers first write failing tests (Red), implement minimal code to pass tests (Green), and then improve code quality while maintaining functionality (Refactor). Students will learn to use Jest testing framework with JavaScript to practice TDD principles on real coding problems. The module covers unit testing fundamentals, test structure and organization, mocking dependencies, and measuring test coverage. TDD is crucial for modern software development as it leads to better code design, fewer bugs, improved maintainability, and increased developer confidence when making changes. By the end of this module, students will understand how TDD transforms the development process from 'code then test' to 'test then code,' resulting in more robust and reliable software. This approach is widely adopted in agile development environments and is essential for professional software developers working in collaborative teams.

Assertion Methods - Jest functions like expect(), toBe(), toEqual() used to verify expected outcomes in tests

title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Uncovering Patterns and Anomalies
description: This module focuses on the critical first phase of any data analysis project: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). Students will learn systematic approaches to examine datasets, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and formulate hypotheses before formal statistical modeling. EDA serves as the foundation for all subsequent analysis, helping analysts understand data structure, quality issues, and underlying relationships. Through hands-on practice with real datasets, students will master both univariate and multivariate exploration techniques using statistical summaries, visualizations, and correlation analysis. The module emphasizes the iterative nature of EDA, where initial findings guide deeper investigation. Students will learn to balance automated discovery tools with manual investigation, developing intuition for when patterns are meaningful versus coincidental. This foundational skill set is essential across all data analysis domains, from business intelligence to scientific research, making it crucial for building analytical thinking and practical data manipulation skills.

key_concepts: Univariate Analysis: Examining single variables through measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape to understand individual variable characteristics
Outlier Detection: Systematic identification of data points that deviate significantly from expected patterns using statistical methods like Z-scores and boxplot analysis
Correlation vs. Causation: Understanding the difference between statistical relationships and causal relationships, including spurious correlations and confounding variables
Data Quality Assessment: Evaluating completeness, consistency, accuracy, and validity of datasets through missing value analysis and data type verification
prerequisite_concepts: Basic statistics: mean, median, mode, standard deviation, and percentiles
Fundamental data types and structures (numerical, categorical, ordinal)
Introduction to Python/R programming and data manipulation libraries (pandas/dplyr)

title: VLAN Implementation and Inter-VLAN Routing
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) implementation and inter-VLAN routing techniques using Cisco switches and routers. Students will learn to segment network traffic logically, enhance security through broadcast domain isolation, and enable communication between VLANs using Layer 3 routing methods. The module covers VLAN creation, port assignment, trunk configuration, VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP), and three primary inter-VLAN routing methods: legacy router-on-a-stick, multilayer switching, and dedicated physical interfaces. Through hands-on laboratory exercises using Cisco Packet Tracer and physical equipment, students will configure VLANs across multiple switches, implement trunk links with 802.1Q encapsulation, and troubleshoot common VLAN-related issues. This foundational knowledge is critical for network segmentation in enterprise environments, preparing students for CCNA certification and real-world network design scenarios where efficient traffic management and security isolation are paramount.
learning_objectives: Students will configure VLANs on Cisco switches by creating VLAN databases, assigning ports to VLANs, and implementing trunk links with 802.1Q encapsulation
Students will implement inter-VLAN routing through configuring router-on-a-stick, multilayer switch SVIs, and routed ports on Layer 3 switches
Students will troubleshoot VLAN connectivity issues using Cisco IOS show commands, ping tests, and VLAN verification tools
key_concepts: VLAN (Virtual LAN) - Logical segmentation of a physical network into separate broadcast domains for improved performance and security
Trunk Links - Connections between switches that carry traffic for multiple VLANs using 802.1Q or ISL encapsulation protocols
Inter-VLAN Routing - Layer 3 routing process that enables communication between different VLANs using routers or multilayer switches
SVI (Switch Virtual Interface) - Virtual Layer 3 interface on a multilayer switch that provides default gateway services for a specific VLAN
VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol) - Cisco proprietary protocol for synchronizing VLAN configuration information across multiple switches
prerequisite_concepts: Basic switching concepts including MAC address tables and frame forwarding
Understanding of OSI model Layers 2 and 3 operations
Cisco IOS command-line interface navigation and basic configuration commands
IP addressing and subnetting fundamentals
Ethernet frame structure and broadcast domains
readings: CCNA 200-301 Official Cert Guide: Chapter 11 - Implementing Ethernet Virtual LANs (Odom, 2020) pp. 243-278
CCNA 200-301 Official Cert Guide: Chapter 17 - VLAN Trunking Protocol (Odom, 2020) pp. 389-412

Packet Tracer Labs: Cisco Networking Academy - VLAN Implementation and Troubleshooting activities

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) Implementation and Best Practices
description: This module introduces students to Test-Driven Development (TDD), a software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing functionality. TDD follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle: writing a failing test (Red), implementing minimal code to pass the test (Green), and then refactoring for better design (Refactor). This approach leads to more reliable, maintainable code with comprehensive test coverage. Students will learn to apply TDD principles using practical examples, understand the psychological and technical benefits of test-first development, and recognize common pitfalls and how to avoid them. The module covers unit testing frameworks, test design patterns, and integration of TDD into modern development workflows. By the end of this module, students will have hands-on experience implementing TDD in real-world scenarios, understanding how it improves code quality, reduces debugging time, and increases developer confidence when making changes to existing codebases.

Students will design comprehensive unit test suites through hands-on practice using JUnit 5 and pytest frameworks for Java and Python respectively
Students will evaluate code quality improvements using TDD metrics including test coverage analysis, cyclomatic complexity measurements, and defect reduction statistics
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD workflow of writing failing tests, implementing minimal code to pass, then improving design through refactoring
Test Coverage: Measurement of how much source code is executed during testing, including statement, branch, and path coverage metrics
Test Doubles: Mock objects, stubs, and fakes used to isolate units under test from external dependencies and control test environments
Regression Testing: Automated tests that ensure new code changes don't break existing functionality, maintained through TDD practices
Refactoring: Systematic code improvement that maintains functionality while enhancing structure, readability, and maintainability

title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM): Implementing Secure Access Controls
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), focusing on implementing robust security controls for cloud resources. Students will learn to design, configure, and manage user identities, permissions, and access policies within AWS environments. The module emphasizes hands-on implementation of IAM best practices, including the principle of least privilege, role-based access control, and multi-factor authentication. Through practical exercises, students will configure IAM users, groups, roles, and policies while understanding how these components integrate to create secure, scalable access management systems. This foundational security knowledge is critical for any AWS practitioner, as improper IAM configuration remains one of the leading causes of cloud security breaches. The module also covers advanced topics such as cross-account access, temporary credentials, and IAM policy troubleshooting, preparing students to handle real-world enterprise scenarios where complex permission structures are required.

key_concepts: IAM Policies - JSON-based documents that define permissions and specify which actions are allowed or denied on AWS resources
IAM Roles - AWS identities with specific permissions that can be assumed by users, applications, or services without permanent credentials
Principal of Least Privilege - Security best practice of granting only the minimum permissions necessary to perform required tasks
Cross-Account Access - Method for securely sharing AWS resources between different AWS accounts using roles and trust policies
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) - Additional security layer requiring users to provide two or more verification factors to gain access

title: VLAN Configuration and Inter-VLAN Routing on Cisco Switches
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) implementation and inter-VLAN routing on Cisco switches. Students will master the fundamental concepts of network segmentation through VLANs, learning how to create, configure, and troubleshoot VLAN implementations in enterprise environments. The module covers VLAN creation, port assignments, trunk configuration, and various inter-VLAN routing methods including router-on-a-stick and Layer 3 switching. Students will gain hands-on experience with Cisco IOS commands, VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP), and switch virtual interfaces (SVIs). This knowledge is critical for network administrators as VLANs are essential for network security, performance optimization, and broadcast domain management in modern enterprise networks. The module emphasizes practical application through lab exercises using Cisco Packet Tracer and real hardware, ensuring students can immediately apply these skills in professional environments.

SVI (Switch Virtual Interface) - Virtual interface on Layer 3 switches that provides routing capabilities for VLANs

title: Wave Interference and Standing Waves
description: This module explores the fundamental principles of wave interference and the formation of standing waves, essential concepts for understanding numerous physical phenomena from musical instruments to quantum mechanics. Students will investigate how waves combine when they meet, examining both constructive and destructive interference patterns. The module emphasizes the mathematical description of superposition and its practical applications in acoustic systems, optical devices, and electromagnetic wave behavior. Through hands-on experiments and computational modeling, students will analyze standing wave patterns in strings, air columns, and electromagnetic cavities. This knowledge forms the foundation for advanced topics including wave optics, quantum wave functions, and resonance phenomena in engineering applications. The module bridges theoretical wave mechanics with real-world applications, helping students understand how wave interference principles govern everything from noise-canceling headphones to laser interferometry used in gravitational wave detection.

Students will evaluate real-world applications of wave interference using computational modeling software to simulate complex interference scenarios
key_concepts: Principle of Superposition - waves combine algebraically when occupying the same space, with amplitudes adding vectorially
Constructive Interference - waves combine to produce maximum amplitude when phase difference is 0, 2π, 4π, etc.
Destructive Interference - waves cancel to produce minimum amplitude when phase difference is π, 3π, 5π, etc.
Standing Waves - stationary interference patterns formed by waves traveling in opposite directions with fixed nodes and antinodes
Resonance - enhanced amplitude oscillations occurring when driving frequency matches natural frequency of the system

title: Risk Management and Mitigation Strategies in Project Management
description: This module focuses on identifying, analyzing, and managing project risks throughout the project lifecycle. Risk management is a critical competency that distinguishes successful project managers from those who merely react to problems as they arise. Students will learn systematic approaches to risk identification, qualitative and quantitative risk analysis techniques, and develop comprehensive risk response strategies. The module emphasizes proactive risk management rather than reactive problem-solving, teaching students to anticipate potential issues and develop contingency plans. Through real-world case studies and practical exercises, students will master the use of risk registers, probability-impact matrices, and Monte Carlo simulations. This module is essential because poor risk management is one of the leading causes of project failure, with studies showing that organizations with mature risk management practices have 40% fewer project failures and 25% lower project costs.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and categorize project risks by conducting systematic risk identification sessions using brainstorming, SWOT analysis, and stakeholder interviews
Students will evaluate risk severity and likelihood through creating probability-impact matrices and calculating expected monetary values for quantitative risk assessment

key_concepts: Risk Register - A structured document that captures identified risks, their characteristics, assessment results, and planned response strategies throughout the project lifecycle
Probability-Impact Matrix - A visual tool that plots risks based on their likelihood of occurrence and potential impact on project objectives to prioritize risk response efforts
Monte Carlo Simulation - A quantitative risk analysis technique that uses statistical modeling to predict the probability of different project outcomes by running multiple scenario iterations

Risk Response Strategies - The four primary approaches to managing identified risks: avoid (eliminate the threat), transfer (shift ownership to third party), mitigate (reduce probability or impact), and accept (acknowledge and monitor)
Residual Risk - The level of risk remaining after risk response strategies have been implemented, requiring ongoing monitoring and potential additional responses
prerequisite_concepts: Project lifecycle phases and milestone management
Stakeholder identification and analysis techniques
Basic understanding of project constraints (scope, time, cost, quality)

title: Wave Interference and Diffraction Phenomena
description: This module explores the fundamental wave behaviors of interference and diffraction, critical phenomena that occur when waves encounter obstacles or interact with each other. Students will investigate constructive and destructive interference patterns, analyze single-slit and double-slit diffraction, and examine practical applications including noise-canceling technology, optical instruments, and wireless communication systems. Through hands-on experiments with laser light, sound waves, and water ripples, students will develop both conceptual understanding and mathematical proficiency in predicting wave behavior. The module bridges classical wave theory with modern applications, demonstrating how these principles underpin technologies from microscopy to radio astronomy. Students will use simulation software to visualize complex wave interactions and conduct laboratory investigations to measure wavelengths and interference patterns. This foundation is essential for understanding advanced topics in optics, quantum mechanics, and electromagnetic wave propagation.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate path differences and predict interference patterns by applying the principles of constructive and destructive interference to double-slit and multiple-slit configurations
Students will analyze single-slit diffraction patterns through laboratory experiments measuring intensity distributions and comparing results to theoretical predictions
Students will evaluate real-world applications of wave interference using mathematical models to explain phenomena in acoustics, optics, and electromagnetic wave systems
key_concepts: Constructive interference - waves combining in phase to produce maximum amplitude when path difference equals integer multiples of wavelength
Destructive interference - waves combining out of phase to produce minimum amplitude when path difference equals odd multiples of half-wavelength
Diffraction - wave bending around obstacles or through apertures, with angular spread inversely proportional to aperture size relative to wavelength
Coherence - degree of correlation between wave phases, essential for observable interference patterns in both temporal and spatial domains
Path difference - geometric difference in distances traveled by waves from sources to observation point, determining interference condition
prerequisite_concepts: Wave properties including wavelength, frequency, amplitude, and phase relationships
Trigonometric functions and their applications to periodic motion and wave mathematics
Basic geometric optics including ray diagrams and Snell's law
Pythagorean theorem and similar triangle relationships for path length calculations

summary: This module provides students with comprehensive understanding of wave interference and diffraction, combining theoretical knowledge with practical applications. Students master the mathematical tools to predict interference patterns while gaining hands-on experience through laser diffraction experiments and computer simulations.
