Students gain proficiency in systematically examining datasets, identifying key patterns and anomalies, and making informed decisions about subsequent analytical approaches. The combination of statistical techniques and visualization methods provides a comprehensive toolkit for understanding data structure and quality. Through practical application with real datasets, students develop critical thinking skills for asking meaningful questions about data and interpreting findings appropriately. These foundational EDA competencies directly support advanced topics in the course including predictive modeling, hypothesis testing, and machine learning, while also building professional skills in data storytelling and reproducible research practices that are highly valued in data science careers.

title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Security Foundation and Best Practices
description: This module provides a comprehensive deep-dive into AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), the cornerstone of AWS security architecture. Students will master the creation, configuration, and management of users, groups, roles, and policies to establish secure access controls for AWS resources. The module emphasizes real-world scenarios including cross-account access, service-to-service authentication, and compliance requirements. Through hands-on labs and practical exercises, students will implement the principle of least privilege, configure multi-factor authentication, and design scalable permission structures. This foundational knowledge is critical for any AWS practitioner, as improper IAM configuration is a leading cause of security breaches in cloud environments. Students will also explore advanced topics including IAM policy evaluation logic, condition keys, and integration with external identity providers. By the end of this module, learners will have the confidence to architect secure, compliant AWS environments and troubleshoot complex permission issues that arise in enterprise cloud deployments.
learning_objectives: Students will design and implement comprehensive IAM policies by creating custom JSON policy documents that enforce least privilege access across multiple AWS services
Students will configure cross-account access scenarios through hands-on creation of IAM roles with trust relationships and assume role policies
Students will evaluate and troubleshoot IAM permission conflicts using AWS CloudTrail logs, IAM Policy Simulator, and Access Analyzer tools
Students will implement multi-factor authentication and password policies through practical configuration of IAM security features and compliance controls
key_concepts: IAM Principals - Users, groups, roles, and AWS services that can make requests to AWS APIs with associated authentication credentials
Policy Evaluation Logic - The systematic process AWS uses to determine permissions through policy types, explicit deny precedence, and condition evaluation
Trust Relationships - The mechanism by which IAM roles define which principals can assume the role through assume role policy documents
Cross-Account Access - Secure method for granting AWS resources in one account permission to access resources in another AWS account
Condition Keys - Contextual information elements in IAM policies that provide fine-grained access control based on request attributes like time, IP address, or resource tags
prerequisite_concepts: Basic understanding of AWS core services (EC2, S3, VPC) and the AWS Management Console navigation
Fundamental JSON syntax and structure for reading and writing policy documents
Basic networking concepts including IP addresses, CIDR blocks, and HTTP/HTTPS protocols
General understanding of authentication vs authorization concepts and security principles
readings: AWS Official Documentation: IAM User Guide - Policies and Permissions (AWS, 2024) sections 1-4, focusing on policy syntax and evaluation
Research Paper: 'Cloud Identity Management Security Analysis' (Chen et al., 2023) - specifically the AWS IAM security model assessment
AWS Well-Architected Framework: Security Pillar - Identity and Access Management section with case studies
AWS Whitepaper: 'IAM Best Practices' (AWS, 2024) - complete document with emphasis on enterprise implementation patterns
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (3 hours reading documentation and whitepapers, 6 hours hands-on labs creating policies and roles, 3 hours capstone project implementing multi-account IAM strategy)
summary: This module establishes critical security foundations by mastering AWS IAM concepts and implementation strategies. Students gain practical experience with policy creation, role-based access control, and security troubleshooting that directly applies to real-world cloud architecture challenges. The hands-on approach ensures learners can immediately implement secure access controls in production environments while understanding the underlying security principles. This knowledge serves as a prerequisite for advanced AWS security services and enterprise cloud governance frameworks, making it essential for cloud architects, security engineers, and DevOps professionals. The module's emphasis on troubleshooting and policy evaluation prepares students for complex enterprise scenarios where multiple policies interact across organizational boundaries.

title: OSPF Dynamic Routing Protocol Configuration and Troubleshooting
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing protocol implementation in Cisco environments. Students will master OSPF fundamentals including hierarchical network design with areas, LSA types, and neighbor relationships. The module emphasizes hands-on configuration of single-area and multi-area OSPF networks, with particular focus on router-id assignment, network advertisements, and area boundary router configurations. Advanced topics include OSPF authentication, route summarization, and stub area implementations. Students will develop critical troubleshooting skills using Cisco IOS show commands and debug utilities to diagnose common OSPF issues such as neighbor adjacency failures, routing table inconsistencies, and convergence problems. Real-world scenarios simulate enterprise network challenges where OSPF scalability and performance optimization are essential. By module completion, students will confidently design OSPF network topologies, implement secure OSPF configurations, and systematically troubleshoot complex routing issues in production environments.
learning_objectives: Students will configure single-area and multi-area OSPF networks by implementing router-id assignments, network statements, and area designations on Cisco routers
Students will analyze OSPF neighbor relationships and LSA propagation through systematic interpretation of show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf database, and show ip route ospf commands
Students will troubleshoot OSPF convergence issues using debug ip ospf events, show ip protocols, and show ip ospf interface commands to identify and resolve adjacency failures
key_concepts: OSPF Areas - Hierarchical network segmentation using Area 0 (backbone) and non-backbone areas to optimize routing table size and convergence time
Link State Advertisements (LSAs) - Database entries containing network topology information, including Router LSAs (Type 1), Network LSAs (Type 2), and Summary LSAs (Type 3)
Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) - Election process on multi-access networks to reduce LSA flooding and optimize neighbor relationships
OSPF Neighbor States - Progression from Down through Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, to Full adjacency establishment
Area Border Router (ABR) - Router connecting multiple OSPF areas, responsible for LSA summarization and inter-area route advertisement
prerequisite_concepts: Static routing configuration and route table interpretation
Subnetting and VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking)
Basic Cisco IOS navigation and interface configuration
TCP/IP fundamentals and IP addressing schemes
Understanding of routing metrics and administrative distance
readings: Textbook chapter: CCNA 200-301 Official Cert Guide Volume 2, Chapter 20-22 'OSPF Concepts and Configuration' (Odom, 2019) pp. 447-521
Cisco Documentation: OSPF Configuration Guide for IOS 15.x - focusing on area configuration and authentication implementation
Online resource: Cisco Learning Network - OSPF LSA Types Deep Dive tutorial and interactive lab scenarios
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 6 hours hands-on lab activities, 2 hours troubleshooting assignments)
summary: This OSPF module bridges theoretical networking concepts with practical Cisco implementation skills essential for network administrators. Students gain expertise in designing scalable hierarchical networks using OSPF areas, configuring secure routing protocols with authentication, and systematically troubleshooting complex routing issues. The hands-on approach ensures graduates can immediately contribute to enterprise network operations, while advanced topics like route summarization and stub areas prepare them for senior networking roles. Mastery of OSPF troubleshooting methodologies using Cisco-specific commands provides critical problem-solving skills valued in production environments. This foundation directly supports progression toward CCNP Enterprise certification and prepares students for real-world network design challenges requiring dynamic routing protocol expertise.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) for Pattern Discovery
description: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the critical first step in any data analysis project, serving as the bridge between raw data and meaningful insights. This module focuses on systematic approaches to understanding data structure, identifying patterns, detecting anomalies, and formulating hypotheses before formal statistical modeling. Students will learn to combine statistical summaries with powerful visualization techniques to uncover hidden relationships in datasets. The module emphasizes practical skills using Python libraries (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn) and R for comprehensive data exploration. Through hands-on exercises with real-world datasets, students will develop the analytical mindset necessary to ask the right questions, recognize data quality issues, and communicate preliminary findings effectively. This foundational skill set is essential for data scientists, analysts, and researchers across all industries, as proper EDA often determines the success of subsequent analysis phases and prevents costly modeling errors.
learning_objectives: Students will conduct comprehensive univariate and bivariate analysis by applying descriptive statistics and creating appropriate visualizations for different data types
Students will identify data quality issues, outliers, and missing value patterns through systematic data profiling techniques and validation checks
Students will generate actionable insights and testable hypotheses using advanced EDA techniques including correlation analysis, distribution assessment, and pattern recognition
key_concepts: Data Profiling - Systematic examination of data quality, completeness, and structure to understand dataset characteristics
Statistical Summaries - Measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape that describe data numerically
Correlation vs Causation - Understanding the distinction between statistical relationships and causal mechanisms in data patterns
Outlier Detection - Methods for identifying anomalous data points that may indicate errors or important exceptions
Data Visualization Grammar - Principles for selecting appropriate chart types and visual encodings based on data types and analytical goals
prerequisite_concepts: Basic statistics including mean, median, standard deviation, and percentiles
Fundamental programming skills in Python or R for data manipulation
Understanding of data types (numerical, categorical, ordinal, temporal)
Basic familiarity with spreadsheet software or data manipulation tools
readings: Textbook chapter: 'Exploratory Data Analysis' from Python for Data Analysis by McKinney (2022) pp. 89-156
Research article: 'The Future of Data Analysis' by Tukey (1962) - foundational EDA philosophy and methodology
Online resource: Kaggle Learn EDA course modules - hands-on exercises with guided datasets
Documentation: Seaborn statistical visualization library - comprehensive plotting techniques for EDA
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (3 hours reading, 6 hours hands-on coding activities, 3 hours capstone EDA project)
summary: This module establishes EDA as the cornerstone of effective data analysis, providing students with both theoretical understanding and practical skills for data exploration. By mastering systematic approaches to data investigation, students will be prepared to tackle complex datasets with confidence and avoid common analytical pitfalls. The combination of statistical thinking and visualization skills developed here directly supports subsequent modules on statistical modeling, machine learning, and data storytelling. Students will leave with a reproducible EDA workflow, a toolkit of proven techniques, and the critical thinking skills necessary to extract meaningful insights from unfamiliar datasets across diverse domains and industries.

title: Situational Leadership: Adapting Your Leadership Style to Context and People
description: This module explores the Situational Leadership Model developed by Hersey and Blanchard, which emphasizes that effective leadership requires adapting one's style based on the competence and commitment levels of team members and the specific context of tasks. Students will learn to diagnose follower readiness, assess situational variables, and flexibly apply four distinct leadership styles: directing, coaching, supporting, and delegating. The module addresses a critical leadership challenge—the myth of one-size-fits-all leadership—by providing a practical framework for making real-time leadership decisions. Through case studies, self-assessments, and role-playing exercises, students will develop the diagnostic skills necessary to read situations accurately and the behavioral flexibility to adjust their approach accordingly. This competency is essential for modern leaders who manage diverse teams, work across cultures, and navigate rapidly changing business environments where rigid leadership approaches often fail.
learning_objectives: Students will diagnose follower development levels by analyzing competence and commitment indicators through structured assessment tools
Students will demonstrate behavioral flexibility by role-playing all four leadership styles (directing, coaching, supporting, delegating) in simulated workplace scenarios
Students will create situational leadership action plans using the Hersey-Blanchard framework to address real workplace leadership challenges
key_concepts: Development Level (D1-D4): The combination of competence (knowledge, skills, experience) and commitment (motivation, confidence) that followers possess for specific tasks
Leadership Style Flexibility: The ability to consciously shift between directing, coaching, supporting, and delegating behaviors based on situational demands
Task-Specific Leadership: The principle that leadership style should vary not just by person, but by the specific task or responsibility being addressed
Follower Readiness Assessment: Systematic evaluation of a team member's capability and willingness to perform particular tasks independently
prerequisite_concepts: Basic understanding of leadership vs. management distinctions
Familiarity with team dynamics and group development stages
Foundational knowledge of motivation theories and individual differences
readings: Textbook chapter: 'Situational Leadership Theory' from Leadership: Theory and Practice (Northouse, 2021) pp. 93-122
Journal article: 'Situational Leadership: A Meta-Analytic Review and Test of Theory' (Thompson & Vecchio, 2009) - focus on empirical validation and limitations
Harvard Business Review article: 'Leadership That Gets Results' (Goleman, 2000) - focus on leadership style repertoire
Online resource: Center for Creative Leadership - 'Adapting Your Leadership Style' interactive assessment and case studies
estimated_workload: 8 hours total (3 hours reading, 3 hours interactive activities and assessments, 2 hours case study analysis and action plan development)
summary: This module equips students with a proven diagnostic framework for adaptive leadership, moving beyond generic leadership advice to provide specific, situation-responsive tools. Students will leave with the ability to assess follower development levels, consciously choose appropriate leadership behaviors, and create targeted development plans for team members. The Situational Leadership Model serves as a bridge between leadership theory and practice, offering immediate applicability in diverse organizational contexts. This foundation prepares students for advanced modules on transformational leadership, cross-cultural leadership, and change management by establishing the core principle that effective leadership requires contextual intelligence and behavioral flexibility rather than adherence to a single leadership philosophy.

title: Newton's Laws of Motion: Forces and Dynamics
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of Newton's three laws of motion, forming the foundation of classical mechanics and our understanding of how forces affect object motion. Students will transition from conceptual understanding to quantitative problem-solving, learning to analyze real-world scenarios involving forces, acceleration, and momentum. The module emphasizes the interconnected nature of Newton's laws through hands-on experiments, mathematical modeling, and practical applications ranging from everyday experiences like walking and driving to engineering applications in aerospace and automotive design. By connecting abstract principles to observable phenomena, students develop critical thinking skills essential for advanced physics topics including energy conservation, rotational dynamics, and fluid mechanics. This module serves as a crucial bridge between kinematics and more complex mechanical systems, establishing the analytical framework students will use throughout their physics education and potential careers in STEM fields.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex force systems by applying Newton's three laws to solve multi-step dynamics problems involving friction, tension, and normal forces
Students will predict and verify object motion through laboratory experiments using force sensors, motion detectors, and video analysis software
Students will construct free-body diagrams using vector notation to represent and calculate net forces in two-dimensional scenarios
key_concepts: Inertia - An object's resistance to changes in motion, directly related to mass and fundamental to Newton's First Law
Net Force - The vector sum of all forces acting on an object, determining acceleration according to F = ma
Action-Reaction Pairs - Equal and opposite forces between interacting objects as described by Newton's Third Law
Free-Body Diagrams - Graphical representations isolating an object and showing all forces acting upon it
Equilibrium - The state when net force equals zero, resulting in constant velocity or rest
prerequisite_concepts: Vector addition and subtraction in two dimensions
Kinematic equations for motion with constant acceleration
Basic trigonometry including sine, cosine, and component resolution
Understanding of mass versus weight distinction
readings: University Physics Chapter 5: Applying Newton's Laws (Young & Freedman, 2019) pp. 124-158
Research article: Teaching Newton's Laws Through Interactive Demonstrations (McDermott, 2018) - focus on misconception identification
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - Forces and Motion: Basics simulation with guided worksheet
Supplementary: Khan Academy Physics - Newton's Laws section videos 1-6 for concept reinforcement
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours laboratory activities and simulations, 3 hours problem sets and assessments)
summary: This module establishes Newton's Laws as the cornerstone of mechanical physics, enabling students to analyze and predict motion in complex systems. Students gain proficiency in mathematical modeling of physical situations while developing intuition about force interactions in everyday life. The combination of theoretical understanding, experimental verification, and problem-solving practice prepares students for advanced topics including energy methods, oscillations, and fluid dynamics. Mastery of these concepts provides the analytical foundation for engineering applications and develops scientific reasoning skills applicable across STEM disciplines. The module's emphasis on connecting mathematical formalism with physical intuition ensures students can both solve quantitative problems and explain phenomena conceptually.

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD): Building Reliable Software Through Testing First
description: This module introduces Test-Driven Development (TDD), a software development methodology that prioritizes writing tests before implementing functionality. Students will learn the Red-Green-Refactor cycle, understand how TDD influences design decisions, and practice writing effective unit tests using modern testing frameworks. The module emphasizes hands-on coding exercises where students experience the iterative nature of TDD and discover how this approach leads to more maintainable, bug-free code. Students will work with real-world scenarios, learning to write meaningful test cases that drive implementation decisions and serve as living documentation. By the end of this module, students will understand when and how to apply TDD principles, recognize the benefits of test-first development for code quality and team collaboration, and be able to implement TDD workflows in their own projects using industry-standard tools and practices.
learning_objectives: Students will implement the Red-Green-Refactor cycle by writing failing tests, making them pass, and improving code structure through guided coding exercises
Students will evaluate code quality and design decisions through analyzing TDD-developed versus traditionally-developed codebases in comparative case studies
Students will create comprehensive unit test suites using Jest and Python unittest frameworks for both new features and legacy code refactoring scenarios
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD workflow of writing a failing test (Red), implementing minimal code to pass (Green), and improving the design (Refactor)
Unit Testing: Writing isolated tests that verify individual functions or methods work correctly, forming the foundation of the TDD approach
Test Coverage and Quality: Understanding the difference between line coverage metrics and meaningful test scenarios that actually validate business logic
Refactoring: The practice of improving code structure and readability without changing external behavior, enabled by comprehensive test suites
Mocking and Stubbing: Techniques for isolating units under test by replacing dependencies with controlled test doubles
prerequisite_concepts: Object-oriented programming fundamentals including classes, methods, and inheritance
Basic understanding of software testing concepts and debugging techniques
Familiarity with at least one programming language (Python, JavaScript, or Java preferred)
Version control systems (Git) and basic command-line operations
readings: Test-Driven Development: By Example - Kent Beck (2002) Chapters 1-8, pp. 1-89
Journal article: The Effects of Test-Driven Development on External Quality and Productivity (Siniaalto & Abrahamsson, 2007) - focus on empirical results
Online resource: Jest Documentation - Getting Started and Testing Asynchronous Code sections
Martin Fowler's blog: Test-Driven Development article and Mocks Aren't Stubs - practical implementation guidance
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (3 hours reading, 6 hours hands-on coding exercises, 3 hours final TDD project implementation)
summary: This module provides students with practical TDD skills that directly impact their ability to write maintainable, reliable software. By experiencing the Red-Green-Refactor cycle firsthand, students develop a testing mindset that influences how they approach problem-solving and code design. The emphasis on hands-on practice with real testing frameworks ensures students can immediately apply these skills in internships and professional development roles. Understanding TDD is crucial for modern software development teams that prioritize code quality, continuous integration, and agile development practices. Students will leave this module with both the theoretical foundation and practical experience needed to advocate for and implement testing-first approaches in their future projects, ultimately making them more valuable team members who contribute to higher-quality software products.

title: Adaptive Leadership: Navigating Complex Organizational Challenges
description: This module focuses on developing adaptive leadership capabilities essential for managing complex, non-routine challenges that lack clear solutions. Unlike technical problems with known fixes, adaptive challenges require leaders to experiment, learn, and mobilize others to discover new solutions. Students will explore Ronald Heifetz's adaptive leadership framework, learning to distinguish between technical and adaptive challenges, manage the adaptive process, and build organizational resilience. The module emphasizes practical skills for leading through uncertainty, facilitating difficult conversations, and creating psychological safety for innovation. Through case studies, simulations, and self-reflection exercises, participants will develop competencies crucial for 21st-century leadership, including emotional regulation under pressure, stakeholder engagement across diverse perspectives, and systematic experimentation. This module is particularly relevant for current and aspiring leaders facing digital transformation, cultural change, crisis management, or strategic pivots where traditional management approaches prove insufficient.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between technical and adaptive challenges by analyzing real organizational scenarios using Heifetz's diagnostic framework
Students will design and facilitate adaptive leadership interventions through role-playing exercises that simulate complex stakeholder dynamics
Students will develop personal adaptive capacity using self-assessment tools, reflection protocols, and peer feedback mechanisms
key_concepts: Technical vs. Adaptive Challenges - Technical problems have known solutions and clear authority structures, while adaptive challenges require learning, experimentation, and changes in values, beliefs, or behaviors
Adaptive Capacity - An individual's or organization's ability to learn, experiment, and adjust in response to complex challenges without losing core identity or mission
Holding Environment - A psychological and social space where difficult conversations and challenging work can occur safely, allowing stakeholders to confront hard realities and explore solutions
Getting on the Balcony - The practice of stepping back from immediate pressures to observe systemic patterns, power dynamics, and underlying issues driving organizational challenges
prerequisite_concepts: Basic leadership theories and styles (transformational, transactional, situational leadership)
Systems thinking and organizational behavior fundamentals
Communication and conflict resolution principles
readings: Core textbook: 'The Practice of Adaptive Leadership' Chapter 3-5 (Heifetz, Grashow & Linsky, 2009) pp. 45-112
Harvard Business Review article: 'Leadership in a Crisis: Responding to the Coronavirus Outbreak and Future Challenges' (Ancona, 2020) - focus on adaptive leadership principles
Case study: 'Netflix's Transformation from DVD to Streaming' via Harvard Business School - examining adaptive leadership during industry disruption
Online resource: Adaptive Leadership Toolkit from Cambridge Leadership Associates - diagnostic questions and intervention strategies
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours activities and discussions, 3 hours individual reflection and case analysis)
summary: This module equips leaders with essential capabilities for navigating today's complex, rapidly changing organizational landscape. Students gain practical frameworks for diagnosing when adaptive rather than technical approaches are needed, along with specific tools for mobilizing stakeholders around difficult challenges. The emphasis on experimentation, learning, and building organizational resilience directly supports the course's broader goals of developing leaders who can thrive in uncertainty. By mastering adaptive leadership principles, students prepare themselves to tackle challenges ranging from digital transformation to cultural change initiatives, ultimately becoming more effective leaders who can guide organizations through periods of significant transition and growth.

title: Amazon EC2: Instance Management and Auto Scaling
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instance management and Auto Scaling capabilities. Students will learn to deploy, configure, monitor, and automatically scale virtual servers in the AWS cloud environment. The module emphasizes practical skills in selecting appropriate instance types, implementing security groups, managing instance lifecycle, and designing resilient applications using Auto Scaling Groups. Through hands-on labs and real-world scenarios, students will understand how to optimize costs while maintaining performance and availability. This foundational knowledge is critical for cloud architects, DevOps engineers, and system administrators who need to design scalable, fault-tolerant infrastructure. The module covers both manual instance management techniques and automated scaling strategies, preparing students to handle dynamic workloads efficiently. By the end of this module, students will be equipped to make informed decisions about compute resources and implement production-ready scaling solutions that respond to changing demand patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy and configure EC2 instances with appropriate security groups and key pairs by completing guided lab exercises
Students will implement Auto Scaling Groups with launch templates and scaling policies through hands-on configuration activities
Students will analyze CloudWatch metrics to optimize instance performance and cost-effectiveness using AWS monitoring tools
Students will design fault-tolerant architectures across multiple Availability Zones by creating multi-tier application deployments
key_concepts: EC2 Instance Types - Categories of virtual machines optimized for different use cases (compute, memory, storage, GPU)
Auto Scaling Groups (ASG) - Service that automatically adjusts the number of EC2 instances based on demand and health checks
Launch Templates - Versioned configuration templates that specify instance settings for consistent deployments
Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) - Service that distributes incoming traffic across multiple EC2 instances for high availability
Security Groups - Virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic at the instance level
CloudWatch Metrics - Monitoring data used to track instance performance and trigger scaling actions
prerequisite_concepts: Basic understanding of virtualization and cloud computing concepts
Familiarity with AWS account setup and IAM user permissions
Knowledge of networking fundamentals including subnets, routing, and firewalls
Basic Linux/Windows command line operations for server management
readings: AWS Documentation: Amazon EC2 User Guide - Instance Types and Launch Templates (AWS, 2024) sections 2-4
Technical Article: 'Auto Scaling Best Practices for Production Workloads' (Wittig & Wittig, 2023) - scaling strategies and cost optimization
AWS Whitepapers: 'AWS Well-Architected Framework - Reliability Pillar' - fault tolerance and multi-AZ deployments
Online Resource: AWS Training Portal - EC2 Fundamentals lab exercises and interactive tutorials
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (3 hours reading, 6 hours hands-on labs, 3 hours assignment completion)
summary: This module establishes essential skills in EC2 instance management and Auto Scaling that form the backbone of AWS infrastructure design. Students gain practical experience in deploying scalable compute resources while understanding cost optimization strategies and fault-tolerance principles. The combination of manual configuration skills and automated scaling knowledge prepares students for real-world cloud operations where they must balance performance, availability, and cost. These competencies directly support the course goal of developing cloud-native thinking and provide the foundation for more advanced topics like containerization, serverless computing, and infrastructure-as-code. Upon completion, students will confidently manage compute resources in production environments and contribute to architectural decisions in cloud migration and modernization projects.

title: Conversion Tracking and Attribution Modeling in Google Analytics 4
description: This module focuses on implementing and analyzing conversion tracking systems within Google Analytics 4 (GA4) to measure business success and understand customer journey touchpoints. Students will learn to configure conversion events, set up Enhanced Ecommerce tracking, and interpret attribution models to optimize marketing spend and improve ROI. The module emphasizes practical implementation of conversion funnels, goal value assignment, and multi-channel attribution analysis. By mastering these concepts, students will be able to provide data-driven recommendations for marketing optimization and demonstrate the direct business impact of digital marketing efforts. This knowledge is essential for digital marketers, analysts, and business owners who need to prove marketing effectiveness and make informed budget allocation decisions across multiple channels and campaigns.
learning_objectives: Students will configure and validate conversion events in GA4 by setting up custom events, importing goals from Google Ads, and implementing Enhanced Ecommerce tracking for at least three different conversion types
Students will analyze customer conversion paths through hands-on examination of attribution reports, comparing first-click, last-click, and data-driven attribution models using real GA4 data

Students will create actionable optimization recommendations using GA4's conversion funnel analysis, identifying drop-off points and calculating conversion rate improvements for specific marketing channels
key_concepts: Conversion Events: User actions that represent valuable business outcomes, configured as measurable goals in GA4 with assigned monetary values and conversion windows
Attribution Modeling: Framework for assigning conversion credit to different touchpoints in the customer journey, including first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven models
Enhanced Ecommerce: Advanced tracking implementation that captures detailed product performance, shopping behavior, and transaction data throughout the purchase funnel
Conversion Funnel Analysis: Method for identifying and analyzing user behavior patterns and drop-off points in the path from initial engagement to conversion completion
prerequisite_concepts: Basic GA4 interface navigation and report interpretation
Understanding of digital marketing channels and campaign structure
Fundamental knowledge of JavaScript and HTML for tracking code implementation
Basic statistical concepts including percentages, ratios, and correlation analysis
readings: Google Analytics 4 Documentation: Conversion Events Setup and Configuration (Google, 2024) - Enhanced Ecommerce Implementation Guide
Digital Marketing Analytics: Making Sense of Consumer Data (Jeffery, 2021) pp. 178-215 - Attribution Theory and Practice
GA4 Help Center: Attribution Modeling and Conversion Paths (Google, 2024) - Data-Driven Attribution Methodology
Journal of Interactive Marketing: Multi-Touch Attribution in Digital Advertising (Li & Kannan, 2023) - Academic research on attribution effectiveness
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours hands-on configuration activities, 3 hours case study analysis and reporting)
summary: Upon completing this module, students will possess the technical skills to implement comprehensive conversion tracking systems and the analytical expertise to interpret attribution data for strategic decision-making. They will understand how to move beyond basic traffic metrics to measure true business impact through GA4's advanced conversion features. This knowledge directly supports the course goal of developing data-driven marketing professionals who can demonstrate ROI and optimize marketing performance across multiple channels. Students will be prepared to handle real-world conversion tracking challenges and provide strategic recommendations based on attribution analysis, making them valuable assets in any digital marketing role.

title: AWS Lambda Serverless Computing: Functions, Events, and Cost Optimization
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of AWS Lambda, Amazon's serverless computing platform that enables developers to run code without provisioning or managing servers. Students will explore the fundamental architecture of Lambda functions, learn to configure triggers from various AWS services, and master deployment strategies using Infrastructure as Code. The module emphasizes real-world application through hands-on labs involving event-driven architectures, API Gateway integrations, and database connections. Special attention is given to cost optimization techniques, performance monitoring, and debugging strategies that are crucial for production environments. Students will work with multiple programming languages supported by Lambda, understand cold start implications, and implement best practices for security and scalability. This module is essential for cloud architects and developers seeking to build modern, cost-effective applications that automatically scale based on demand while reducing operational overhead.
learning_objectives: Students will design and deploy Lambda functions with appropriate runtime configurations by implementing event-driven processing scenarios using AWS CLI and AWS SAM
Students will configure Lambda integrations with API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB, and CloudWatch through hands-on labs building a complete serverless web application
Students will optimize Lambda performance and costs using monitoring tools like X-Ray, CloudWatch Insights, and AWS Cost Explorer to analyze execution patterns and resource utilization
key_concepts: Function as a Service (FaaS) - serverless computing model where code executes in stateless containers managed entirely by the cloud provider
Event-driven architecture - system design pattern where Lambda functions respond automatically to triggers from AWS services like S3 uploads, DynamoDB changes, or API calls
Cold start latency - initial delay when Lambda creates new execution environments, affecting performance and requiring optimization strategies
Execution context reuse - Lambda's mechanism for reusing containers across invocations to improve performance and reduce initialization overhead
Concurrent execution limits - AWS-imposed restrictions on simultaneous function executions that require capacity planning and throttling management
prerequisite_concepts: Basic understanding of cloud computing principles and AWS core services (EC2, S3, IAM)
Proficiency in at least one programming language (Python, Node.js, Java, or C#)
Fundamental knowledge of RESTful APIs and JSON data structures
Basic familiarity with command-line interfaces and version control systems
readings: AWS Official Documentation: AWS Lambda Developer Guide - Chapters 1-3 (Amazon Web Services, 2024) focusing on function configuration and event sources
Research Paper: 'Serverless Computing: Current Trends and Open Problems' (Castro et al., 2023) - sections on performance optimization and cost analysis
AWS Well-Architected Framework: Serverless Applications Lens (AWS, 2024) - complete document covering design principles and best practices
Online Tutorial Series: AWS Lambda Hands-On Labs (A Cloud Guru, 2024) - modules 1-5 covering basic to intermediate implementations
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading documentation and research papers, 6 hours hands-on labs and coding exercises, 2 hours completing serverless application project)
summary: This module equips students with practical serverless computing skills essential for modern cloud development. By mastering Lambda functions, event-driven architectures, and cost optimization techniques, students gain competencies directly applicable to enterprise cloud solutions. The hands-on approach ensures students can immediately implement serverless patterns in real projects, while the focus on monitoring and debugging prepares them for production challenges. This foundation connects to broader course objectives of building scalable, cost-effective cloud architectures and prepares students for AWS certification paths. The skills learned here integrate seamlessly with subsequent modules on microservices, API design, and cloud-native application development, making this a cornerstone module for comprehensive AWS cloud expertise.

title: E-commerce Tracking and Enhanced E-commerce Analysis in Google Analytics
description: This module focuses on implementing and analyzing e-commerce data in Google Analytics, specifically covering Enhanced E-commerce tracking capabilities. Students will learn to set up comprehensive e-commerce measurement that goes beyond basic transaction tracking to include user behavior throughout the entire purchase funnel. The module addresses critical business questions such as product performance analysis, shopping behavior insights, checkout funnel optimization, and revenue attribution across marketing channels. Enhanced E-commerce provides granular data about user interactions with products, from initial product impressions through purchase completion, enabling data-driven decisions for online retailers. Students will work with real e-commerce scenarios to configure tracking, interpret shopping behavior reports, analyze product performance metrics, and create actionable recommendations for improving conversion rates and revenue. This advanced tracking methodology is essential for e-commerce businesses seeking to optimize their online sales performance and understand customer purchase patterns in detail.
learning_objectives: Students will implement Enhanced E-commerce tracking code by configuring data layer variables and Google Tag Manager tags for a sample online store
Students will analyze shopping behavior flow reports through hands-on interpretation of checkout funnel data and product interaction metrics
Students will create comprehensive e-commerce performance dashboards using Google Analytics reporting interface and custom segments for different customer types
key_concepts: Enhanced E-commerce Data Layer - structured format for passing detailed product and transaction data to Google Analytics
Shopping Behavior Analysis - methodology for analyzing user interactions from product discovery through purchase completion
Product Performance Metrics - key indicators including product revenue, conversion rate, cart-to-detail rate, and buy-to-detail rate
E-commerce Attribution Models - frameworks for assigning conversion credit across multiple marketing touchpoints in the customer journey
prerequisite_concepts: Basic Google Analytics account setup and navigation
Understanding of Google Tag Manager fundamentals
Familiarity with JavaScript and HTML basics
Knowledge of standard e-commerce metrics and KPIs
readings: Google Analytics Help Documentation: Enhanced E-commerce Implementation Guide (Google, 2024) - complete setup instructions
Research Article: E-commerce Analytics and Customer Journey Optimization (Chen & Rodriguez, 2023) - behavioral analysis frameworks
Online Resource: Google Analytics Academy - E-commerce Analytics Course modules 3-5
Case Study: Shopify E-commerce Tracking Best Practices (E-commerce Analytics Quarterly, 2024) pp. 45-62
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (3 hours reading, 6 hours hands-on implementation activities, 3 hours analysis assignments)
summary: This module equips students with advanced e-commerce tracking capabilities that extend far beyond basic transaction measurement. By mastering Enhanced E-commerce implementation and analysis, students gain practical skills in comprehensive online retail performance measurement. The hands-on approach ensures students can immediately apply these techniques to real-world e-commerce scenarios, making them valuable assets for digital marketing teams and online retailers. The module's focus on actionable insights from shopping behavior data directly supports broader course goals of data-driven decision making and advanced Google Analytics proficiency. Students completing this module will confidently configure complex e-commerce tracking systems and extract meaningful business intelligence from detailed customer purchase journey data.

title: Big O Notation and Algorithm Complexity Analysis
description: This module introduces students to algorithm complexity analysis using Big O notation, a fundamental concept for evaluating algorithm efficiency. Students will learn to analyze time and space complexity of algorithms, enabling them to make informed decisions when selecting or designing algorithms for real-world problems. The module covers mathematical foundations of asymptotic notation, practical analysis techniques for common algorithm patterns (loops, recursion, divide-and-conquer), and comparative analysis of data structures. Through hands-on coding exercises and complexity calculations, students will develop the analytical skills necessary to predict algorithm performance at scale. This knowledge is essential for technical interviews, system design, and building efficient software solutions. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical application, preparing students to optimize code performance and communicate algorithm trade-offs effectively in professional settings.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate time and space complexity for iterative and recursive algorithms by applying Big O, Omega, and Theta notation rules
Students will compare algorithm efficiency across different input sizes through empirical testing and mathematical analysis
Students will optimize existing code implementations using complexity analysis to identify bottlenecks and select appropriate data structures
key_concepts: Big O Notation: Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
Time Complexity: Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size
Space Complexity: Analysis of memory usage required by an algorithm including auxiliary space and input storage
Asymptotic Analysis: Mathematical framework for describing algorithm behavior with very large inputs
Best/Average/Worst Case: Different scenarios of algorithm performance based on input characteristics and distribution
prerequisite_concepts: Basic programming constructs (loops, conditionals, functions)
Fundamental data structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues)
Elementary discrete mathematics and logarithms
Recursion and recursive thinking
readings: Textbook chapter: Introduction to Algorithms, Ch 3 'Growth of Functions' (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 43-68
Journal article: 'Teaching Algorithm Analysis: A Practical Approach' (Smith, 2023) - focus on pedagogical methods and common misconceptions
Online resource: Khan Academy - 'Asymptotic Notation' interactive lessons with visualization tools
Supplementary: GeeksforGeeks 'Analysis of Algorithms' tutorials - practical examples and code implementations
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours programming exercises, 3 hours complexity analysis assignments)
summary: This module establishes critical analytical skills for algorithm evaluation that students will use throughout their computer science education and careers. By mastering Big O notation and complexity analysis, students gain the ability to predict algorithm performance, make data-driven decisions about implementation choices, and communicate technical trade-offs effectively. The combination of mathematical rigor and practical application prepares students for advanced coursework in algorithms, data structures, and system design, while also building competencies essential for technical interviews and software engineering roles. These foundational concepts directly support the course's broader goals of developing computational thinking and problem-solving expertise.

title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Implementing Secure Access Control
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), the cornerstone service for securing AWS cloud environments. Students will master the creation and management of users, groups, roles, and policies to implement the principle of least privilege across AWS resources. The module emphasizes hands-on implementation of real-world security scenarios, including cross-account access, service-to-service authentication, and compliance requirements. Understanding IAM is critical for any AWS practitioner, as it underpins security for all other AWS services. Students will learn to navigate common IAM challenges such as policy troubleshooting, permission boundaries, and access key rotation. The module combines theoretical security principles with practical AWS console and CLI operations, preparing students to design and implement robust access control systems that meet enterprise security standards while maintaining operational efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will design and implement comprehensive IAM policies by analyzing business requirements and applying least privilege principles through hands-on policy creation exercises
Students will configure cross-account access scenarios through practical labs involving IAM roles, trust policies, and temporary credential management
Students will troubleshoot IAM permission issues using AWS CloudTrail, IAM Policy Simulator, and Access Analyzer tools to identify and resolve access problems
Students will establish automated IAM best practices by implementing password policies, MFA enforcement, and access key rotation using AWS CLI and CloudFormation templates
key_concepts: IAM Policies - JSON documents that define permissions specifying allowed or denied actions on AWS resources
IAM Roles - AWS identities with permission policies that determine what the identity can and cannot do, designed to be assumed by trusted entities
Principal of Least Privilege - Security concept of granting only the minimum permissions necessary to perform required tasks
Cross-Account Access - Mechanism allowing users or services from one AWS account to access resources in another AWS account securely
IAM Policy Evaluation Logic - The process AWS uses to determine whether to allow or deny a request based on identity-based, resource-based, and permission boundary policies
Temporary Security Credentials - Short-term access credentials obtained through AWS Security Token Service (STS) for enhanced security
prerequisite_concepts: Basic understanding of AWS core services (EC2, S3, VPC) and how they interact
Fundamental knowledge of cloud computing concepts and shared responsibility model
Basic familiarity with JSON syntax and structure
Understanding of basic networking concepts and HTTP/HTTPS protocols
Familiarity with command-line interfaces and basic scripting concepts
readings: AWS Well-Architected Framework Security Pillar: Identity and Access Management (AWS Documentation, 2024) - Focus on IAM best practices sections
Cloud Security and Privacy: An Enterprise Perspective on Risks and Compliance: Chapter 7 - Identity Management (Mogull, 2019) pp. 145-178
AWS Documentation: IAM User Guide - Policies and Permissions section (AWS, 2024) - Complete policy language reference
Research Paper: Access Control in Cloud Computing (Zhang et al., 2020) Journal of Cloud Computing Security - Focus on role-based access control implementation
AWS IAM Best Practices Whitepaper (AWS Security Team, 2024) - Emphasis on automated security controls and monitoring
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 6 hours hands-on labs, 2 hours policy design assignment)
summary: This module establishes students as competent IAM practitioners capable of securing AWS environments through proper access control implementation. By combining security theory with extensive hands-on practice, students develop both the conceptual understanding and practical skills needed to design, implement, and maintain secure cloud access systems. The emphasis on real-world scenarios and troubleshooting prepares students for common challenges they'll face in professional AWS environments. Mastery of IAM concepts serves as the foundation for advanced AWS security topics and professional certifications, while the practical skills gained directly translate to improved security posture in any AWS deployment. Students will leave this module with confidence in their ability to implement enterprise-grade access controls and contribute meaningfully to cloud security initiatives.

title: Risk Identification and Assessment Techniques
description: This module provides comprehensive training on systematic risk identification and assessment methodologies essential for successful project management. Students will master both qualitative and quantitative risk analysis techniques, learning to proactively identify potential project threats and opportunities before they impact project outcomes. The module emphasizes practical application of PMBOK Guide risk management processes, focusing on Risk Identification (11.2) and Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis (11.3). Through hands-on exercises using real project scenarios, students will develop expertise in facilitating risk identification workshops, creating comprehensive risk registers, and applying probability-impact matrices to prioritize risks effectively. This module is critical for PMP certification preparation as risk management accounts for significant portions of the PMP exam and represents one of the most challenging aspects of project execution in today's complex business environment.
learning_objectives: Students will identify comprehensive project risks by facilitating structured brainstorming sessions and applying systematic risk identification techniques including SWOT analysis, assumption analysis, and expert interviews
Students will assess and prioritize identified risks through creation of probability-impact matrices and risk scoring methodologies aligned with organizational risk tolerance
Students will develop complete risk register documentation using standardized templates that include risk descriptions, probability assessments, impact analysis, and preliminary response strategies
key_concepts: Risk Register - Comprehensive document containing identified risks, their characteristics, probability, impact, and planned responses
Probability-Impact Matrix - Visual tool that plots risks based on likelihood of occurrence and potential impact magnitude to prioritize risk response efforts
Monte Carlo Simulation - Quantitative risk analysis technique using statistical modeling to predict project outcomes based on risk variable distributions
Expected Monetary Value (EMV) - Decision-making technique that calculates expected financial impact by multiplying probability by monetary impact
Risk Breakdown Structure (RBS) - Hierarchical decomposition of potential risk sources organized by risk categories
prerequisite_concepts: Project scope definition and work breakdown structure fundamentals
Basic understanding of project constraints (time, cost, quality, resources)
Stakeholder identification and analysis techniques
Project lifecycle phases and knowledge area integration
readings: PMBOK Guide 7th Edition: Chapter 2 - Performance Domain: Uncertainty (PMI, 2021) pp. 45-68
Journal article: Effective Risk Assessment in Complex Projects (Hillson, 2020) - focus on identification methodologies and assessment frameworks
Online resource: PMI.org Risk Community of Practice - Risk Register Templates and Best Practices documentation
estimated_workload: 8 hours total (3 hours reading, 3 hours workshop activities, 2 hours risk register assignment)
summary: This module equips students with essential risk management competencies that directly support PMP certification requirements and practical project leadership effectiveness. Students will gain confidence in facilitating risk identification sessions, creating defensible risk assessments, and communicating risk information to stakeholders and senior management. The systematic approach to risk identification and assessment learned here provides the foundation for subsequent risk response planning and monitoring activities. These skills are immediately transferable to workplace projects and represent core competencies that distinguish effective project managers. Mastery of these techniques significantly improves project success rates and prepares students for advanced risk management responsibilities in complex organizational environments.

title: Risk Identification and Assessment Techniques: Advanced Topics 1
description: This module focuses on systematic approaches to identifying, analyzing, and documenting project risks during the project planning phase. Students will learn to apply structured risk identification techniques, conduct qualitative and quantitative risk assessments, and create comprehensive risk registers. The module emphasizes practical application of PMI's risk management standards and tools, including probability and impact matrices, risk categorization frameworks, and stakeholder-driven risk identification workshops. Understanding these concepts is critical for PMP certification and real-world project success, as effective risk identification can prevent 60-80% of project failures. Students will work with realistic project scenarios to practice identifying both obvious and hidden risks, assess their potential impact on project objectives, and prioritize risks for further analysis and response planning. This foundational knowledge directly supports the PMI's Project Risk Management knowledge area and prepares students for advanced risk response strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will identify project risks using at least five systematic techniques including brainstorming, SWOT analysis, and expert interviews by completing a comprehensive risk identification workshop
Students will assess risk probability and impact through qualitative analysis tools including probability/impact matrices and risk categorization frameworks
Students will create a complete risk register using PMI templates that documents risk descriptions, categories, probability ratings, impact assessments, and risk scores for a given project scenario
key_concepts: Risk Identification Techniques - Systematic methods including brainstorming, Delphi technique, SWOT analysis, checklist analysis, and assumptions analysis to discover project uncertainties
Qualitative Risk Analysis - Process of prioritizing risks by assessing probability of occurrence and impact on project objectives using standardized scales and matrices
Risk Register - Central document that captures identified risks, their characteristics, assessment results, and planned responses throughout the project lifecycle
Probability and Impact Matrix - Grid tool that maps risk probability against potential impact to calculate overall risk scores and prioritization rankings
Risk Categories - Structured classification system (technical, external, organizational, project management) that ensures comprehensive risk coverage and facilitates analysis
prerequisite_concepts: Project Management Framework - Understanding of project phases, processes, and knowledge areas as defined in PMBOK Guide
Stakeholder Management Basics - Knowledge of stakeholder identification and engagement principles for effective risk identification sessions
Project Scope and Objectives - Clear understanding of project deliverables, success criteria, and constraints that risks may impact
readings: PMBOK Guide 7th Edition: Chapter 2 - Project Risk Management (PMI, 2021) pp. 397-459
Journal article: Risk Identification Effectiveness in IT Projects (Jiang & Klein, 2020) - focus on systematic vs. ad-hoc identification methods
PMI Practice Standard: Risk Management Template Library - downloadable risk register and assessment templates
Online resource: PMI.org Risk Community of Practice - case studies on industry-specific risk identification techniques
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 5 hours activities, 3 hours assignments)
summary: This module equips students with essential risk management skills that form the foundation of successful project delivery. By mastering systematic risk identification techniques and assessment tools, students develop the analytical mindset required for PMP certification and effective project leadership. The practical focus on creating risk registers and conducting assessments prepares students for immediate application in their current roles while building toward advanced risk response planning modules. These competencies directly address PMI's emphasis on predictive risk management and stakeholder value delivery, making this module crucial for both certification success and career advancement in project management.
original_title: Risk Identification and Assessment Techniques

title: Advanced Data Structures: Binary Trees and Balanced Trees
description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of tree-based data structures, focusing on binary trees, binary search trees (BSTs), and self-balancing trees including AVL and Red-Black trees. Students will master the theoretical foundations of these hierarchical data structures while developing practical implementation skills. The module emphasizes understanding time and space complexity trade-offs, tree traversal algorithms, and the critical importance of maintaining balance for optimal performance. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithmic analysis, students will learn when and why to choose specific tree structures for different applications. This knowledge is essential for efficient database indexing, compiler design, file systems, and many other computer science applications. The module bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical software development skills, preparing students for advanced algorithms courses and real-world programming challenges where efficient data organization and retrieval are paramount.
learning_objectives: Students will implement binary search trees with insertion, deletion, and search operations by writing complete Java or Python classes with proper error handling
Students will analyze tree traversal algorithms (inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order) through both recursive and iterative implementations
Students will design and implement AVL tree rotations and rebalancing algorithms using step-by-step visual debugging techniques
Students will evaluate time complexity scenarios for balanced vs unbalanced trees by conducting empirical performance analysis with datasets of varying sizes
Students will solve real-world problems requiring tree data structures through project-based assignments involving file system simulation or expression parsing
key_concepts: Binary Search Tree (BST) - A hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, with left subtree values less than parent and right subtree values greater than parent
Tree Traversal Algorithms - Systematic methods for visiting all nodes in a tree: inorder (left-root-right), preorder (root-left-right), postorder (left-right-root), and level-order (breadth-first)
AVL Tree Balancing - Self-balancing binary search tree where heights of left and right subtrees differ by at most one, maintained through rotations
Tree Rotations - Local restructuring operations (single and double rotations) that preserve BST property while improving balance
Red-Black Tree Properties - Self-balancing BST with color-coded nodes following specific rules to guarantee O(log n) operations
prerequisite_concepts: Basic data structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues) and their operations
Recursion and recursive problem-solving techniques
Big O notation and algorithm complexity analysis
Object-oriented programming concepts (classes, inheritance, encapsulation)
Basic mathematical concepts including logarithms and proof techniques
readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 12 'Binary Search Trees' and Chapter 13 'Red-Black Trees' (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein, 4th Edition) pp. 287-348
Journal article: 'An algorithm for the organization of information' (Adelson-Velsky & Landis, 1962) - historical foundation of AVL trees
Online resource: VisuAlgo.net - Interactive Binary Search Tree and AVL Tree visualizations with step-by-step algorithm execution
Supplementary reading: 'Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis' Chapter 4 'Trees' (Weiss, 4th Edition) pp. 131-186
estimated_workload: 18 hours total (6 hours reading, 8 hours coding activities, 4 hours assignments)
summary: This module equips students with comprehensive knowledge of tree-based data structures, essential for efficient data organization and retrieval in computer science applications. By mastering binary search trees and balanced tree variants, students gain critical skills for database systems, compiler design, and algorithm optimization. The combination of theoretical understanding and practical implementation prepares students for advanced coursework in algorithms and data structures while providing immediately applicable skills for software development. Students will emerge with the ability to choose appropriate tree structures for specific problems, implement complex balancing algorithms, and analyze performance characteristics of hierarchical data organization methods.

title: Newton's Laws of Motion: From Concepts to Real-World Applications
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of Newton's three laws of motion, serving as the foundation for classical mechanics and engineering applications. Students will move beyond memorizing formulas to develop deep conceptual understanding through hands-on experiments, problem-solving scenarios, and real-world case studies. The module emphasizes the interconnected nature of the laws and their universal applicability, from everyday phenomena like walking and driving to complex systems like spacecraft navigation and sports biomechanics. Through interactive demonstrations, mathematical modeling, and laboratory work, students will learn to identify forces, analyze motion, and predict outcomes in various physical systems. This understanding is crucial for advanced physics topics including energy, momentum, rotational dynamics, and serves as prerequisite knowledge for engineering disciplines. The module integrates historical context, showing how Newton's insights revolutionized our understanding of the physical world, while connecting to modern applications in technology and space exploration.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex multi-body systems by applying Newton's three laws systematically to predict motion and force interactions
Students will solve real-world physics problems through free-body diagram construction and mathematical force analysis
Students will evaluate the validity of Newton's laws using experimental data collection and graphical analysis techniques
Students will design and conduct controlled experiments to demonstrate each law of motion using laboratory equipment and digital sensors
key_concepts: Newton's First Law (Inertia): Objects at rest stay at rest and objects in motion continue in uniform motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced force
Newton's Second Law (F=ma): The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass
Newton's Third Law (Action-Reaction): For every action force, there exists an equal and opposite reaction force acting on different objects
Free-body diagrams: Visual representations showing all forces acting on a single object, essential for problem-solving
Net force and equilibrium: The vector sum of all forces and the conditions required for zero acceleration
Inertial reference frames: Coordinate systems in which Newton's laws are valid, moving at constant velocity relative to each other
prerequisite_concepts: Vector addition and subtraction in two dimensions
Basic trigonometry (sine, cosine, tangent functions)
Kinematics equations for constant acceleration
Concepts of mass, weight, and gravitational force
Unit conversion and dimensional analysis
readings: Physics: Principles with Applications Chapter 4: Dynamics - Newton's Laws of Motion (Giancoli, 2016) pp. 83-112
Research article: Teaching Newton's Laws with Interactive Simulations (Henderson & Martinez, 2019) - focus on conceptual understanding methods
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - Forces and Motion Basics module with guided worksheet activities
Supplementary reading: The Principia Chapter 1 excerpts (Newton, translated edition) - historical context and original formulations
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading and video content, 4 hours laboratory experiments, 2 hours problem sets, 2 hours simulation activities)
summary: This module establishes the fundamental framework for understanding motion and forces that governs everything from molecular interactions to planetary orbits. Students develop both conceptual mastery and practical problem-solving skills that are essential for success in advanced physics courses and STEM careers. The emphasis on experimental validation and real-world applications helps students appreciate the power and elegance of Newton's insights while building confidence in mathematical modeling of physical systems. Upon completion, students will possess the analytical tools needed for topics like energy conservation, momentum, and rotational mechanics, while gaining appreciation for the scientific method and the historical development of physics. The skills developed in systematic problem-solving, experimental design, and quantitative reasoning extend far beyond physics, supporting success in engineering, medicine, and other technical fields.

title: Newton's Laws of Motion: From Concepts to Real-World Applications: Advanced Topics 1
description: This module provides students with a comprehensive understanding of Newton's three laws of motion and their practical applications in everyday life and engineering contexts. Students will explore the fundamental principles governing how objects move and interact, developing both conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills. The module emphasizes the interconnected nature of the laws, demonstrating how they form the foundation of classical mechanics. Through hands-on experiments, mathematical problem-solving, and real-world case studies, students will gain proficiency in applying these laws to analyze motion in various scenarios including projectiles, collisions, and systems with multiple forces. The module bridges theoretical physics with practical applications, showing how these 17th-century principles continue to govern modern technology from automotive safety systems to spacecraft navigation. Students will develop critical thinking skills by analyzing complex scenarios, identifying relevant forces, and predicting outcomes using Newton's laws as analytical tools.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex motion scenarios by systematically applying Newton's three laws to predict and explain object behavior
Students will solve quantitative problems involving force, mass, and acceleration through step-by-step mathematical calculations and free-body diagrams
Students will design and conduct controlled experiments using laboratory equipment to verify Newton's laws and measure physical quantities
Students will evaluate real-world applications by connecting theoretical principles to practical examples in technology, sports, and transportation
key_concepts: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia): An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity unless acted upon by an unbalanced net force
Newton's Second Law (F=ma): The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass
Newton's Third Law (Action-Reaction): For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force acting on different objects
Free-body diagrams: Visual representations showing all forces acting on a single object, essential for problem-solving
Net force: The vector sum of all forces acting on an object, determining the object's acceleration according to Newton's second law
prerequisite_concepts: Vector addition and subtraction, including graphical and component methods
Basic algebra and trigonometry for force calculations and component analysis
Concepts of mass, weight, and the distinction between scalar and vector quantities
Understanding of motion descriptors: position, velocity, and acceleration from kinematics
readings: University Physics: Chapter 4 'Newton's Laws of Motion' (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 104-142
Research article: 'Misconceptions in Newton's Laws Among Engineering Students' (Henderson, 2019) - focus on common conceptual errors
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - 'Forces and Motion' modules for virtual experimentation
Case study: NASA Technical Publication - 'Newton's Laws in Spacecraft Design' pp. 15-28
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (4 hours reading, 4 hours laboratory activities, 2 hours problem sets, 2 hours simulation exercises)
summary: This module establishes Newton's laws as the cornerstone of classical mechanics, enabling students to analyze and predict motion in diverse contexts. By mastering these fundamental principles, students develop essential problem-solving frameworks applicable throughout their physics education and beyond. The combination of theoretical understanding, mathematical application, and experimental verification prepares students for advanced topics in mechanics, engineering, and related fields. The emphasis on real-world connections demonstrates the enduring relevance of these principles in modern technology and scientific research, fostering appreciation for the predictive power of physical laws and their role in technological innovation.
original_title: Newton's Laws of Motion: From Concepts to Real-World Applications

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) Implementation and Practices
description: This module introduces students to Test-Driven Development (TDD), a software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing code. TDD follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle, where developers first write failing tests (Red), implement minimal code to pass tests (Green), and then improve code quality while maintaining functionality (Refactor). This approach fundamentally changes how developers think about code design, leading to more modular, testable, and maintainable software. Students will learn to write effective unit tests, understand test coverage metrics, and apply TDD principles to real-world programming scenarios. The module emphasizes practical application through hands-on coding exercises using popular testing frameworks. By mastering TDD, students develop disciplined coding habits, improve debugging skills, and create more reliable software systems. This methodology is widely adopted in agile development environments and is considered essential for modern software engineering practices. Students will also explore how TDD integrates with continuous integration pipelines and contributes to overall software quality assurance processes.
learning_objectives: Students will implement the Red-Green-Refactor cycle by writing failing tests, minimal passing code, and refactored solutions for at least three programming problems
Students will analyze code quality improvements through hands-on comparison of TDD versus traditional development approaches using metrics like cyclomatic complexity and test coverage
Students will create comprehensive unit test suites using JUnit (Java) or pytest (Python) frameworks for a medium-complexity application with at least 80% code coverage
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The three-phase TDD process of writing failing tests, implementing minimal code to pass, and improving code structure
Unit Testing: Automated tests that verify individual components or functions in isolation from the rest of the system
Test Coverage: Measurement of how much source code is executed during testing, typically expressed as a percentage
Test Doubles: Mock objects, stubs, and fakes used to isolate units under test from their dependencies
Refactoring: The process of restructuring existing code without changing its external behavior to improve readability and maintainability
prerequisite_concepts: Object-oriented programming fundamentals including classes, methods, and inheritance
Basic understanding of software debugging and error handling techniques
Familiarity with at least one programming language (Java, Python, C#, or JavaScript)
Understanding of software development lifecycle and basic version control with Git
readings: Textbook chapter: 'Test-Driven Development' in Clean Code by Robert Martin (2008) pp. 123-142
Research article: 'On the Effectiveness of Test-first Approach to Programming' by Erdogmus et al. (2005) - empirical evidence for TDD benefits
Online resource: Kent Beck's Test-Driven Development tutorial series on Martin Fowler's website - practical TDD examples and best practices
Documentation: JUnit 5 User Guide sections 1-4 or pytest documentation chapters 1-3 depending on chosen language
estimated_workload: 12 hours total (3 hours reading, 6 hours hands-on coding activities, 3 hours completing TDD project assignment)
summary: This module equips students with practical TDD skills that directly improve software quality and development efficiency. By learning to write tests first, students develop a deeper understanding of requirements and create more focused, maintainable code. The hands-on approach ensures students can immediately apply TDD principles in their programming projects and future software development roles. The module connects to broader course goals by reinforcing software engineering best practices, preparing students for collaborative development environments, and establishing foundations for advanced topics like continuous integration and automated deployment.
